Garima Bajpai is the Founder of the DevOps Community of Practice in Canada. Martin Reynolds is a Field CTO at Harness. Patrick Debois is an AI Product Engineer and AI Native Dev Advisor. Gunnar Grosch is a Developer Advocate at Sinch. Renato Losio is an InfoQ Staff Editor, Cloud Expert, and AWS Data Hero.

InfoQ Live is a virtual event designed for you, the modern software practitioner. Learn from extraordinary speakers driving change and innovation.

Presented by: Kiran Gangadharappa - Engineering Advisor at Harness, and Scott Davis - Senior Engineering Manager at Harness

Renato Losio: Today we'll discuss how AI is changing software delivery, so from code generation to production, how AI-assisted software delivery is changing in our crazy times.

In this roundtable, we are going to discuss how AI is changing the way organizations are going to build, test, secure, deploy, operate software. What is the real challenge today? We are all familiar with AI in general now and how it's changing every aspect of our developer life, but one of the challenges we discuss maybe less is how is integrating AI into the broader engineering lifecycle while maintaining quality, security, and reliability.

My name is Renato Losio. I'm an editor at InfoQ. I'm joined today by four experts coming from different companies, different sectors, different countries. I'd like to give a chance to each one of them to introduce themselves and share their journey, and why they are part of this panel today.

Patrick Debois: My name is Patrick Debois. I have some history in DevOps and CI/CD. I currently help Tessl with building a software factory for your coding agents.

Martin Reynolds: I'm Field CTO at Harness. I spend most of my time working with our customers on everything that we're talking about today. Everything that's after code, build, test, secure, deploy, operate. Also, I say recently, a few months back, I also now co-host a podcast called ShipTalk. We talk about everything that's going on with AI that's in the news.

Garima Bajpai: I'm Garima Bajpai. I bring 25 years of leadership experience leading software development organizations at an enterprise level. Lately, I'm being more known for my work with AI and how AI would scale when it comes to software development. I'm more interested and intrigued by community-driven initiatives, community-driven InnerSourcing work, as well as hackathons, micro and mega hackathons, which we have been doing.

Gunnar Grosch: I'm Gunnar. I'm a developer advocate at Sinch. I have also spent about 25 years or something in the industry building software, working with developer communities. These days, I build and talk a lot about AI agents in production, and working with Sinch, obviously that means a lot of conversational AI in different ways. I also have a podcast with some friends, called, Yells at Cloud.

Renato Losio: How is AI already changing software delivery in your organization? We are all familiar with developers using coding assistants. We are familiar with maybe agents in pure development. We hope we are not all just vibe coding, but how is it really already affecting software delivery?

Patrick Debois: We're probably going through these phases that everybody went through. Like you described, first it was your completion, then it was your coding agent. A lot of people still do that with their Claude and their OpenAI working together on their laptop. Then we started seeing, there's a lot of context. We're putting knowledge back somewhere in skills and more information, so the agents become better. We improve the harness. That's all good. I would call that our solo level, team shared level working together. About six or seven months ago, we switched to using a central pipeline, what we call the factory in general, where we're all working more through filing tickets, the agents take care of it, so it's less running on our laptop. That created a different dynamic in the company from the solo dev to actually product, engineering, sales, support, all working together. That's the transformation that we went through. I think that's not unique.

Renato Losio: You mentioned before the entire conversational chat and whatever. What's your take on this?

Gunnar Grosch: I think we're seeing a similar thing that Patrick just described. There are different parts of the development lifecycle that are changing. I think part of it is about trusting it to be able to hand off things. I think we're seeing it in stages. One part that is easy to handle is the research part. Before you start writing code, previously you had to usually do a lot of research, figure out how a codebase worked or how an API worked and so on. Those are things that are easy to hand off, let agents do, and then you get the result back and you can take part of it. Same with the other end of the lifecycle, where you deploy, you test, you iterate, and you have that loop over and over again. Also, fairly easy to hand off to agents and let them take part of it.

What I'm still seeing a lot is that the step in between, that's still where developers or engineers are engaged. They're still doing a lot of the work in that in-between, so handing off the initial work, handing off that last leg of the work, but still doing a lot of the work in between. I think a lot of it comes down to trust, being able to actually hand off that entire work. It's a bit scary.

Renato Losio: I don't know, really on a personal experience, I can say that if you talk to many practitioners it's, yes, we are experimenting with it. We are doing that. We are doing delivery using agents. When you ask, so are you doing that in production completely and trust, or you did this step? Not yet. Or we have a proof of concept or we have in a small project, but that's a big leap. I think we'll come back often to that.

Martin Reynolds: I think that's something that comes up quite often, especially work with quite a lot of regulated environments, and the trust is a big thing. I think if you had good governance on your delivery process before and you can make sure you can apply it in the same way to agents, then they'd fail the same way a person would fail. The mechanism might not be exactly the same, but I think you need the governance set up the same way, so that they should have things like scoped credentials, policies, approvals, audit trail, so they're not free-roaming agents. Coming back to that gap that was mentioned, it's interesting, because I think you're right. There are things like code review that seems to be an ever-increasing challenge, like test generation, even auto-fix of failed builds and failed deployments, or the ever eternally-growing number of CVEs that seem to exist in the world thanks to AI.

It's like, here's a load more CVEs in your build. All of those things you can use AI to do. You can use it to help you with code review. You can use it to help with test generation. I think it is evolving. One of the fun things about working where I work is that we build a lot of software, and we've been tackling a lot of these problems as we go along.

Garima Bajpai: I actually wanted to add a few things here, because, again, as Patrick and Gunnar alluded to the fact that with AI, the individual productivity has improved. That's a no question that code is no longer the scarce capability. That's a given thing in an enterprise ecosystem. What we see, again, different companies, different communities, different experiences. There are three things which I think are standing out for us. I also come from a critical infrastructure background as well, very controlled and regulated environment. Our testing capabilities, our testing matrices, we see that they are broken now, because we are leading to more next-generation test matrices where the validity for implementing it on a probabilistic LLM application, testing must shift from a statistical threshold to golden data points. LLM-as-judge rubrics comes into play. The second aspect is security. Security must transition to runtime. As DevOps advocates, we have advocated for shift left capabilities, but I think it's also more shift right at this point in time.

The third part, which also from an enterprise perspective, we have been seeing and are struggling with, FinOps, how to adopt token economics at scale. When you work with a 20,000-developer ecosystem, it becomes a very substantial amount of your capability, like how your token economics would shift and how FinOps becomes a very integral part of your ecosystem. These three things I think we have seen that now people are being more conscious about, and we are also seeing governance control levers, guardrails, around our delivery agents to make it more holistic.

Patrick Debois: I love that you're bringing up the compliance, the cost. The way that we started thinking about this is you're building code. Like you said, it's easier. That's fine. Like Martin says, you need to have tests. That is still important. Good engineering practices don't go away. Observabilities that you need, you need the scaling. You need all those pieces in there as well, because what they do is actually they improve the code and they reduce the likelihood of having issues. That's the first piece of you give better context, you write tests, you get less issues. That's one way of dealing with it. The second piece that you see now more and more in people's workflows is a risk analysis. The agent has done all the steps. They added tests. There was an adversarial review. They got a better result. Now it's the fact like, ok, can I actually push this change through?

What is the impact? A simple documentation change is completely different than you touching the authentication piece in your code. People are using ways to look at, ok, should this go directly or not? That is similar to what we did before. A user says this is important, this is not important. This is a risk as well. Then the third piece, very DevOps, like you said, Garima, is when it moves to production, what is the impact? We had the likelihood, the risk, and then the impact. Many people tell me, we don't look at the code anymore. I ask them, ok, what's your application? It's some blog site. It's some random small thing, or it's experimental. Of course, you don't look at it. It has a different risk profile of you pushing something out. That's fine in that. Now imagine your risk is higher. What we did in the past is we architecture around the failure.

What if the machine goes down, can it quickly get back up? Can we restore the data fast? What is the impact? You mitigate in your architecture not just if the risk is there, but it happened, and it was the same with the humans. This just now applies more and more. A lot of people just focus on optimizing the results, but they don't think about risk. It's really hard to get that decision in an organization. What is the risk that we're willing to take? What is the impact of this? I want people to think more about those pieces as well than just saying like, everything will go automatically. No, there's a gradation of what you do. Some things are manual review. Some things are automatic through. That's the balancing act that a lot of teams are now struggling with.

Gunnar Grosch: I think it's funny because these are the same discussions that we've had throughout the years with different types of change with DevOps. Those similar type discussions, how much to automate and should we be able to push things into production and so on. I've spent a lot of time talking about resilience through the years and chaos engineering. I think Netflix was the common example there. Just like we said then, not everyone is Netflix. You don't have to do chaos engineering tests in production just like now. Not everyone is Anthropic and has to have fully automated agents that are pushing 30,000 PRs per day or whatever that number is. Everyone has to start somewhere. You don't have to start with everything just being fully automated. You probably shouldn't even be close to it.

Renato Losio: Until now, we had some good best practices. We wanted to make sure that the code was understandable for the next developer joining the line, usually, with a few exceptions. That has always been the approach in software, enterprise, open source, and whatever. What's going to be the future there? We say for the pipeline, we're going to deploy it. We're going to have tests. We're going to have anything automated. Do you think readable and human understandable code is still something we should expect, or do we just rethink that already and move the problem to just deploy?

Martin Reynolds: I've had a lot of discussions about this, and I do think it's a super interesting topic because we've also seen that the most effective users of AI are the more senior developers, generally, which is almost counterintuitive. It feels like you still need to understand how it all works. I think ultimately, we will get to the bit where we're not reading any code. I don't think that's going to happen for a while, but I think there is. I would lean into what Patrick was saying about the levels of risk. If you've written a bunch of code for a blog site, do I care to read all of that? No. If it's my banking application that handles all my transactions, I want to still be able to understand that, and especially when it goes wrong. Sometimes you just need to be able to still read it when it goes wrong.

I don't think we're at a point yet where we can 100% trust what's generated. We know it generates more issues. We know that there's been an increase in live issues for code. We know that there's more CVEs in it. We know that we're finding CVEs faster. All of those things tell me that we should still be able to read it at the moment. Future, maybe 10 years down the line, current rate, 2, who knows? We might get to that. I think it will come in stages, and risk is a big factor for that.

Renato Losio: Do you still read all the code?

Patrick Debois: Again, it depends on the feature, what I do. I've set this up to understand better. That debate about like, should we just let the agent loose? I do TDD, and we could say, don't do it. It helps the agent because the agent can run tests and can verify what it built, that it actually worked. This is just an example. Should it write docs? Of course, because if the docs are up to date, it actually helps the context of the agent. It feels like in a way that what was good for human engineering practices actually helps the AI do a better job. If you have multiple ways of standards in your code, the AI is getting confused. If you clean that up, it will do a better job. The code is one thing, we're getting to in some tooling about reviewing the intent while not looking at the code.

Formal verification is making a comeback in a way that we specify what we want, and then it can actually verify that with the tests. That is like a new layer of how do we look at that. We also make the AI agents and the coding agents prove us that it works. They create videos. They show it. They have to really convince us. Does that mean that we're looking at all the code? Again, it depends if I really care about one specific part. If it passes all the tests and it passes all the things, it might be as good as a human would do before.

Garima Bajpai: What my experience goes is, when you take code at an enterprise scale level, of course, we'll have to shift the needle in how we are thinking about the syntax of the code and the two capabilities which we have started to take very seriously is semantic layer. How do we build code through AI and AI agents and how the semantics of that has been built around it. We have invested time in that. The second aspect is forensic, because we don't want code to have vulnerabilities and we don't want to shift the problem from software development to software maintenance. These two components are very critical for our harness layer. Then we also have some circuit breakers. When AI agent starts to write enormous amount of code, so what we have found is AI has been notoriously poor in handling those kinds of large context windows. We ensure that when there is a lot of code being written by agents, we have circuit breakers and we have to have the human reviewers in place.

Renato Losio: We love automatic tests. We love the thing that now it's possible to create them, and we can delegate testing and PR approval to AI. That's great. I have the feeling on a personal level that is, I like to go back to the standard usual example of the photography that in the past used to be you couldn't do many pictures. You had 24, 36 maximum with a camera, so you were quite careful in designing them properly. Maybe they were not the best one, but you were putting some effort. Now, I saw an explosion, at least in the project I follow, of tests. Now the coverage of tests is great and that's really a great improvement. It's like digital photography, you can create so many. The problem is that there's really a lot of noise. Of course, the big question is, do you use a very specialized AI tool on the market or you build your own, or you just use some regular testing framework? Gunnar, you mentioned before AI testing. I don't know what you use or what you do in that space.

Gunnar Grosch: I'm not using anything that's specific or newer frameworks. It's following the same practices as before, both when it comes to the regular frameworks that we use and then for the more resilience testing and so on as well. No changes in it, but just like you said, with agents, the test coverage looks very different these days. In apps or services where we would create a smaller number of tests before, now all of them has hundreds of tests. The test coverage looks very different with the help of agents.

Patrick Debois: I do two very small things. One is I say files can't be bigger than 200 lines, which restricts the pieces of the change, like Garima was saying. It's not like the big chunks. Then the other one is I actually say you need to have 99% test coverage. In my hook, I actually verify that with my test coverage tool. If it's not complying, either I need to split up the tests due to the smaller files, or creates the test. That's like two nudges that I use very practically to keep that more under control. Indeed, like Gunnar says, it's the same tooling, but we're nudging AI in a way that it uses those tools more efficiently.

Martin Reynolds: I think that's really interesting. I don't know if anybody remembers this. I was talking to somebody recently, and they were talking about the table game where you have your path to production, and you're moving things through, and every so often you roll the dice, and it says that step in the process failed. I'm picking up really on your small changes thing here. Funnily enough, whether you're using AI for all the steps or not, a big change that fails still has the same blast radius and the impact on the down the line and how much gets shipped and the shipping, lots of small steps on that production line when something fails, the impact and the blast radius is still way smaller, whether you're using AI or not. Almost going back to what you were saying at the start of, the old principles still apply. They still work. There's a reason that we developed them over the years. Just because we have AI doesn't mean that we should just throw them out the window.

Garima Bajpai: One thing which I think is changing from our perspective is definition of done, because what we have done is we have added more checkpoints, which are centric to correctness, quality, semantics. Also ensuring that the definition of done, not only the code output is correct, but also how the code would live or be maintained in the long term. These factors are very important. I think in the ongoing basis, we will see the shift happening in that area as well.

Renato Losio: AI can deliver code at a pace that cannot be matched by humans, so humans reviewing the code is becoming a bottleneck. What would be your insights how to increase throughput? I would say don't fire people. That's on a very personal level. I don't know if anyone has really faced already that problem of like the human side being the bottleneck in deployment.

Martin Reynolds: That's pretty much the status quo right now. It doesn't really matter where in that chain you look, because we've talked about quite a lot of things already, but for some organizations, the human bottleneck is at the PR stage, but it could be in writing tests and making sure that they're safe. It could be in security triage and remediation. There's just a whole bunch of areas that rely on humans right now. There is this constant layering of, can we use AI to help accelerate this? Most of these systems were designed for changes that happened at human writing code speeds. We've accelerated everything at the front, and we need to make sure that we can safely accelerate those things to the right. I also agree. I do think it's a layered thing and it is by risk.

Patrick Debois: That's the clue. You can't approve all the things. You can ask for proof. You can ask to do it better. Those are things that will help the reviewer move it on the verification more on the intent layer because you don't need the code. You can verify on those pieces. Those are all accelerators. At a certain moment you say, ok, these things can go up, and that's a big chunk done. Now, unfortunately, like you said, more CVEs. Now it's like you have to maintain your context. That's work again. There's the factory PRs. That builds up. The clue is getting that risk analysis, and not just risk analysis, but the architecture that it can mitigate whatever risk that you're doing. I think that's probably the next phase in dealing with that.

Gunnar Grosch: It is simple math if the number of PRs are doubled, if you don't double the number of reviewers, you need to do it in a different way. You will have to then either do a shallower review, which probably isn't the right way to do it. It's about then, like you said, look at the risk, what are the things you need to actually dive deeper into when it comes to reviews? The solution isn't to automate it with AI either, because reviewing AI, is not the answer to the question.

Martin Reynolds: I know internally, and for some of our customers, we take a risk-based approach. We don't use the same AI for coding that we use for reviewing, just like you wouldn't use the same person to review.

Renato Losio: That's a very important point. Sometimes we take for granted that people don't do that.

Martin Reynolds: You don't want to mark your own homework.

Gunnar Grosch: You want to, but you shouldn't.

Martin Reynolds: You want to, but that's not effective. We take a risk-based approach. We review the PR if we think that is a low-risk PR. Then we might allow AI to accept that PR because the risk is low, based on a whole bunch of metrics, not just, I think this is low, but what's the stability of this? How much has this code been reworked? What happened in the last 10 deployments? Is it a stable part of the system that's changed? Taking all of those things into account, we can then say, this is low-risk, medium, or high-risk. Actually, low risks don't need a person. Then you can also use AI to help you solve that problem, and say, there's a thousand lines of code changed here. It's mostly updated versions of dependencies, but here's the bit of the code that you actually need to look at in the diff, not all the other bits, because they're files that were touched because we updated the version of a dependency.

Here's the bit that actually changed in the functional. You can help accelerate that and take away some of the stress, because there's nothing worse than a big diff, which is why I'm still a massive advocate of small code changes. When you get a diff with a thousand lines, humans are rubbish at reading a thousand-line changes. They are good at saying, I know this is the important bit, and now I can focus on it. It's the same for everything else, but I just want to give this as an example.

Gunnar Grosch: There are things that AI is great at when it comes to reviews. It can do style reviews, for instance, look at patterns. It can see conventions and make sure that the code is then readable for the next person or the next agent and so on. Because, like you said before, Patrick, if all the code looks different, it makes it harder for agents as well. You can use agents to then review for following your style and your conventions.

Patrick Debois: I want to give one example, which I think is a cool addition to this thing. Imagine you have two code changes and two different people have asked it. Imagine this is your billing thing that calculates the total of your invoice. There's a total function that you say, don't do it in dollars, but do it in dollar cents. It creates like a PR, everything passes, it's logical, that code change is happening. At the same time, there is a person asking for, I want a new invoice report, and that will use the total function, but they don't want to display it in euro cents or dollar cents. They want to still have it in dollars in general. If both PRs land after each other, they are mergeable, they are correct, but they're both semantically incompatible. Because the one change started with the concept of still understanding that it was calculated in dollars, and the other one is changing this concept while the other was landing. Now we have to look at PRs, if they're ok, not just on code merging and being correct as code, but being compatible on intent.

Renato Losio: It's a requirement. If the two requirements together still make sense.

Patrick Debois: Which I don't think we're really checking right now in our reviews.

Garima Bajpai: I think this is an excellent point. We started to also measure intent to production metrics. This is my personal belief that in no time, intent will become the backlog and bottleneck. Because there will be a lot of code into production, but if you are trying to measure mean time from intent to production, the intent becomes the bottleneck.

Renato Losio: How do you introduce AI tools into a highly regulated space with rigid IT security configurations, such as financial institutions and the public sector?

Martin Reynolds: Introducing AI is no different to introducing any other tool. You need to make sure that you have the right controls in place, the right governance in place. All those checks and balances need to be there. It is not different to any other tool. You need to follow those same processes. I would say now, certainly most regulated organizations that we work with, they have a very defined process for introducing AI into their environments. They know what the checks and balances are that they need to add in to do that. In general, governance is the core. I think this might sound weird, but it's more important on the delivery side than it is on the coding side. Because on the coding side, the agent is living on your machine and in the code repository and doesn't have access to production environments, doesn't have access to things that can break, probably doesn't have access to a whole bunch of sensitive information.

When you put that and agents are running in your actual production environments, deploying software, creating infrastructure, whatever it is that they're doing, running tests against that infrastructure, suddenly there's a whole bunch of things that you need in a regulated environment that don't exist. Executing agents in production brings a different level to what is required of an agent that is writing code against a codebase on a developer's machine, and that you have to build in the guardrails to be able to get the trust.

Garima Bajpai: I'll add to some of the points which, Martin, you have mentioned, because you're spot on. There are guardrails, governance, there are teams which are specialized in a regulated ecosystem which works on a central level, how this whole ecosystem should evolve, and there has to be guardrails, for the risk which we carry and the blast radius which we have. There's another risk which has been introduced when we talk about AI as a technology, because AI is evolving very fast. What I have seen in my experience is that with regulated sector, there is a high risk of shadow AI being adopted because there is a central governance which says, apply the brakes. Then people are seeing that the democratization of the technology is happening. I think it's a very interesting challenge when it comes to regulated sectors. Now, what we have done, and I have talked to several communities about this problem, the velocity trap is real.

Everybody is creating agents on their machines, and the experimentation has come to production level. What we have done is we have community-led InnerSourcing frameworks where a particular persona which works as an agent and which fulfills 80% of the jobs, then these agents can live in a centralized ecosystem and everybody can spin off those agents. That way the risk of having shadow AI on your laptop, on your machines experimenting with different tools, it's getting limited because it's a community-led InnerSourcing framework which we have experimented. I don't say that it works for every enterprise and every segment, but again, this is a very interesting problem to solve.

Gunnar Grosch: Before joining Sinch, I worked for AWS for many years, and part of that time was when all of this started, with the AI boom we're in right now. Regulated industries, that was definitely one of the most common questions at that time. The way that question was framed back then was usually that we can't use OpenAI or Anthropic or even AWS, so how can we run all of this ourselves? Luckily, we've been able to move past that as an industry, I think. These days, most of these providers have made it possible for regulated industries to run these AI tools. It is about governance, just like Martin said. Once again, I want to emphasize what he said as well, that there are two different parts. One is the AI tools we as engineers or developers or users are using. That's one part of it, and that's just pure governance.

I think that these types of organizations, they have to do it if they haven't already to avoid the shadow AI that Garima talked about as well. That's where you'll end up otherwise with people running Gemini on their personal phones or whatever it might be. The other part is using AI in their production workloads. I think we're past the point where that was a problem as well. There are so many ways of still being compliant and doing that these days as well. It's just that they need to be able to actually be able to audit things. They need to be able to see whatever they are building is doing. That's where a lot of organizations across the board are failing today. Many AI agents that I see in production today, they are black boxes. People don't know what their agent is doing.

Garima Bajpai: One more thing which is very interesting is it's still a heterogeneous technology. People are looking at their own agents, their own integration points. There is some level of standardization which has happened with MCP, for example. Agents, by and large, are heterogeneous. I think industry experts right in this panel and beyond this panel would work towards standardization because that is the need of the hour. How to make this ecosystem homogeneous, interoperable, because that is something I would look forward to for another one or two years from now.

Patrick Debois: The reason, Martin, why I was shaking my head when you said it's predominantly there, is that when we were developing traditional software, there was also the piece of what pieces of third-party software we could pull in into our codebases, what licenses, and things like that. There is a piece that ends up in that world as well of vetting and making sure things are ok and secure there as well. Now, there's the layer of context that has similar characteristics. You can install skills from a registry. You can download skills, but they can contain scripts and so on. There's a new piece that a lot of enterprises might not be thinking about as this new piece that they need to control as well. It's not just a coding agent. It's whatever you pull in there. Is it PII data? Like, whatever pieces? That is also contributing to whatever upstream your production is doing.

It could be equally harmful if you do it in the bad way, what ends up where to what systems? It might not be the shadow IT, but it's like even in their existing workflows, it might not be mitigated yet on that level because there are new pieces, new threats, the prompt injection, all those pieces, which still feels as an industry we haven't really gotten around as dealing with that governance in a good way.

Renato Losio: I like the idea of asking the agent to prove that its work is correct and convince us of it. Besides tests, what other thing can we ask the agents to do to make human review easier, faster, and more complete, as opposed to just keeping when risk is low?

Patrick Debois: One simple thing we do is we have it record the workflows, so the end-to-end workflows, and we say, ok, make sure that it's viewable. I just walk it through it. I'm not just looking at the code, but I actually see it in action functional-wise, which is probably a lot easier. If it is a bigger chunk of work, we ask it to split up the review into multiple pieces. It's not just showing us the div. We're saying, ok, guide us through the div, almost like you would do a slideshow of what has changed. What did you do? The understanding that it helps us do that in our language. It's not just that it understands that it did a good job, but we have a narrative, a set of questions like, what did you do for this? What did you do for that? It could still lie, of course, but it helps us understand better what the change was doing.

Garima Bajpai: One more thing, I'll tell you, start from the foundational piece, the foundation layer, where is your knowledge base? You create or construct a knowledge base. Based on that, you have a harness which talks about what semantics would be there, what forensic would be there, what is your definition of done. Pieces of the puzzle which are changing. It makes the human reviewer's job easier because there is a harness layer, which is working already on these agents, which is making sure that the foundational pieces of the puzzle are correct. It's quality assured. There are security elements embedded. There are guardrails. Then the human reviewers comes in play with a long-term hat on top of their head saying that, ok, how these 20 microservices would exist or be maintainable in the longer run. That is what the role of a human reviewer would be in some time.

Renato Losio: In a zero-trust environment, what deterministic controls, metrics should be added to ensure AI tools only do what they should, and is measurable?

Martin Reynolds: For me, in zero-trust, it's purely about scoped credentials, though. If you're giving an agent very specific scoped credentials, probably time-limited as well, then it's the same constraints you would give a person. "I need to perform this task. This is the very explicit permissions I need to perform that task. Here is your temporary credentials for performing that task. I know that they're assigned to this agent, which is running as part of this pipeline". Then all of that is audited. In that zero-trust environment, you're doing exactly the same thing that you would do for a human. #10023. Your Agent Aced the Task. Will It Do It Again?

Your agent works in rehearsal, but during the live demo, it takes a different path and fails the same task.

That is embarrassing onstage. In production, it is a reliability problem: a workflow that succeeded once may fail the next time a user makes the same request. For mission-critical work, such as reconciling a financial transaction or checking a contract for an obligation, that can be a showstopper.

Most benchmarks hide this variability behind an average. On AppWorld, a ReAct agent using GPT-4.1 succeeded on 77.4% of runs across five repetitions. But it succeeded in all five runs for only 53.0% of tasks — a 24.4-point consistency gap.

Most benchmarks report the first number. We built a way to measure the second — and improve it.

In an earlier post, we introduced ALTK-Evolve — a system that turns an agent's own past trajectories into reusable guidelines, distilled automatically and injected back at inference time. It measurably improves task success, but those results only asked the average-case question too. This post introduces consistency guidelines, a new guideline type in altk-evolve built on top of a diagnostic tool we call the Consistency Analyzer, that targets this gap directly.

Standard agent evaluation reports Mean@k: run a benchmark k times, average the pass rate. Often k=3, sometimes just 1. It's the number on every leaderboard, and it's what "77% accurate" means in practice.

Mean@k answers "how good is this agent, on average?" It does not answer the question a real user cares about: will it still be good if I ask this exact question again? For that you need Pass^k: the fraction of tasks where the agent succeeds on all k runs.

⚠️ Pass^k is not Pass@k. The familiar Pass@k is optimistic — it asks whether at least one of k attempts succeeded, the right question when you can verify and retry. Pass^k is its pessimistic mirror image: every attempt must succeed. Same letters, opposite question. Pass^k ≤ Mean@k ≤ Pass@k, always.

A ReAct agent backed by GPT-4.1 posts a Mean@5 of 77.4% — genuinely strong. But Pass^5 is only 53.0%. Nearly a quarter of the benchmark consists of tasks the agent can sometimes solve and sometimes can't, with nothing about the task changing between runs. We call this gap — Mean@k minus Pass^k — the consistency gap.

This isn't a capability problem you fix with a bigger model. It's an orthogonal axis: an agent can be capable and inconsistent at the same time.

Every time an LLM agent decides something — which API to call, what argument to pass, whether to retry — that decision comes out of a probability distribution over next tokens. What matters is the shape of that distribution. A sharp one puts most of its mass on a single token: the runners-up are far behind, and the same choice comes out run after run. A flat one spreads comparable mass across several near-tied tokens, and which one wins is close to a coin flip.

The shape decides how much noise it takes to change the outcome. Sharp distributions are resilient — GPU floating-point non-associativity, request batching, and other platform-side effects nudge the numbers slightly, but nowhere near enough to reorder a clear winner. Flat distributions are vulnerable to exactly that nudge: near-ties may reorder under small perturbations. And because a trajectory chains dozens of decisions, a small per-step chance of flipping compounds into a large chance that some run goes differently. That's where a 24-point gap comes from.

This is also why the problem survives your decoding settings. Greedy decoding and a fixed seed both govern how a distribution gets turned into a token — they say nothing about the distribution itself. On a hosted endpoint the probabilities shift slightly from run to run, so the same prompt to the same model at temperature zero can still resolve a near-tie one way today and the other way tomorrow.

Our setup: the ReAct agent runs at temperature 0.0, so none of the variance above is ordinary sampling.

Which turns the problem into a search: which steps in a given trajectory were the flat ones — and what do you do about them once you know?

Consistency guidelines come out of a two-stage pipeline that plugs into ALTK-Evolve's existing machinery — with a new source signal driving what gets written.

1. Detect — the Consistency Analyzer. Given one recorded trajectory, the analyzer replays each decision step through controlled resampling, measuring how much the model's output actually varies at that point. Concretely, that's one additional model call per decision step, done once offline — issued with the sampling parameter set to draw k completions at once (k=5 by default) — replayed against the already-recorded context, not new tool calls, not new environment interactions, and not a second end-to-end rollout of the task. This yields a consistency score per decision step that is written into a scorecard to pinpoint exactly which decisions are at risk of flipping on the next run. Detection is fully black-box — no logits, no model internals, no instrumentation beyond the trace you already have.

2. Generate — targeted guidelines. Every flagged step becomes a candidate consistency guideline in the standard ALTK-Evolve format, so it slots into the existing storage and retrieval pipeline. Here's a real example, generated by GPT-4.1 from a trajectory of the AppWorld task "How many activities are done in my bucket list as per my SimpleNote note?":

[Guideline 1] When counting checkbox-style markers in note content, use a line-anchored regex match rather than a plain substring count — note titles often repeat the marker symbol in a legend line.

[Guideline 2] Always verify search results for note queries by checking for multiple matches and confirming the correct note before proceeding.

Nothing here is task-specific trivia. String-counting bugs and unverified search results are decision points that show up with high uncertainty across many AppWorld tasks. That's the point: the analyzer targets instability, not failure — so it catches steps the agent happened to get right this time but could easily get wrong next time.

Watch the 2-minute demo — five parallel runs of the agent split 3-2 on this task because of agent uncertainty about the counting strategy, then run again after these guidelines in context: all five agree.

We evaluated on AppWorld test_normal (168 tasks) with a ReAct agent on GPT-4.1, generating consistency guidelines from a single baseline trajectory per task and testing them on 5 fresh runs.

Mean@5 (%), aggregate — same scale as Pass^5 above.

The consistency gap is cut roughly in half. Aggregate Pass^5 rises 53.0% → 69.0% while Mean@5 rises 77.4% → 81.0%, narrowing the gap between "looks capable" and "can be counted on" from 24.4pp to 12.0pp. Nearly a third of previously-inconsistent tasks become tasks the agent passes on every single run.

The middle and hard tiers gain most. Medium +22.9pp (+44% relative), Hard +14.3pp (+45% relative) — effectively tied in relative terms, with Medium ahead absolutely. Easy gains +12.2pp, having had the least room. This is consistency guidelines doing what they're designed to do: finding and stabilizing the specific decision points where an agent's own uncertainty was leaking into the outcome.

Mean@5 never drops. Preserving average accuracy was a hard requirement, not a nice-to-have: a system that boosts Pass^5 by trading away Mean@5 would just be shifting unreliability around, not fixing it. Mean accuracy holds or improves at every difficulty level.

Applied to a different but related task in the same AppWorld scenario — another variant of the scenario the guidelines were mined from — consistency guidelines still lift Pass^5 by +13.0pp, only 3 points below the same-task number. A guideline derived from one run isn't just patching that run; it's capturing something that transfers.

The sharper evidence comes from a weaker model, gpt-oss-120b. Same-task Pass^5 rose +6.0pp from a much lower baseline (10.1% → 16.1%) — and, interestingly, the similar-task generalization number (+8.7 pp) actually exceeded the same-task gain, suggesting the guidelines were capturing genuinely reusable failure patterns rather than memorizing one trajectory's specifics.

Try the ALTK-Evolve — the open-source repo now includes the Consistency Analyzer and consistency-guideline generation used in these experiments — or read the technical report on arXiv for the complete methodology.

If accuracy numbers you can't reproduce on your own tasks sound familiar, we'd like to hear about it — concrete examples of flip-prone behavior in your own agents are exactly the kind of feedback that shapes what we build next. Open an issue or a discussion.

Great perspective on agent reliability. Measuring consistency alongside accuracy seems especially important as AI agents move into workflows where reproducibility matters. The Consistency Analyzer approach is a fascinating way to identify unstable decisions without requiring full task replays.

The useful split is the one most dashboards still refuse to print: Mean@k answers “how good is this agent on average?” Pass^k answers “will the same request still succeed if I ask again?”

Once you’ve watched a trajectory chain dozens of near-tied tool choices, a strong average with a wide consistency gap is exactly the demo that fails live. Capability and consistency are orthogonal — buying a bigger model can lift Mean without closing the gap.

What I want teams to take from the Consistency Analyzer framing is operational, not the guideline machinery itself: treat flip-prone decision steps as first-class eval targets. One offline resample pass over a recorded trace is a cheaper reliability signal than another end-to-end leaderboard screenshot.

Practical ask for anyone shipping agents from this: do you report Pass^k (even k=3) next to Mean@k in the release gate, and do you refuse the “stable” label when the consistency gap is still large on your hard tier?

Reproducible reliability will not remove disagreement about which guidelines to inject. It will make the disagreement about the right metric.

Thanks, and you've landed on exactly the operational takeaway we hoped for: flip-prone decision steps should be eval targets in their own right. Beyond that, knowing where they are also turns the eval into a diagnostic: a consistency gap tells you that an agent is unreliable, while the flip-prone steps tell you where and why.

On your release-gate question: we'd strongly encourage it, and k=3 is a sensible default. A few things we'd suggest to anyone adopting Pass^k as a gate:

I'd like to understand your closing point better. In our experiments, we didn't choose among individual guidelines: for each new task, we injected the guidelines derived from the most similar task. I'm curious where you see the disagreement about which guidelines to inject arising.

#10022. tokenizers v1: encode, decode and scaling, measured

The tokenizer has not historically been the bottleneck within ML workflows. Compute-wise, tokenization is light compared to the heavy modeling happening in the rest of the pipeline. Yet, in some cases, it has rapidly become key to accelerating (or slowing down) your machine learning work.

As models become faster and workloads scale, that balance begins to shift. Training on massive datasets, serving many concurrent requests, or repeatedly processing long inputs can put enough pressure on the tokenizer that it starves the model of data.

This is why we have chosen to heavily focus on performance for the upcoming version 1 of tokenizers. Tokenization should be light and should scale with your workflow. Your GPUs should never sit idle waiting for the CPU to complete its tokenization.

In this article, we look at what makes v1 faster than v0.23, often by tens of times.

This work was entirely possible thanks to the rest of the ecosystem. Tokenization is a very active area of open source work, and libraries such as gigatoken, tiktoken, kitoken, tokie, fastokens, wordchipper and ai-tokenizer, as well as many others, have each pushed on what a fast tokenizer can be. We read that work, and several of the ideas below reached us because another project showed they were worth trying.

Before this refactor, tokenizers was nowhere near the performance it could have had, so contributing to it may not have seemed worth it. With this refactor, we hope to make clear that we intend tokenizers to be a library worth contributing to.

We also thank IBM, NVIDIA, and the ExecuTorch team for contributing patches and helping us test across a wide range of hardware to broaden platform support.

We showcase results for the release candidate of tokenizers v1 against other widely used alternatives. We go over single-threaded, multi-threaded, scaling across threads, per-model comparison, per-language comparison, latency, decoding throughput, memory heap, as well as crate size.

We run this from the tokbench repository, and add a command to rerun the benchmarks on your hardware if you would like to do so.

v1 will produce the same token IDs as v0.23. The goal was to preserve the output, the API, the vocabulary and the merge ranks, and improve everything that can be improved. That includes breadth. The library stays general across tokenizer families rather than specialising on BPE, so v1 loads everything v0.23 loaded.

A tokenizer converts text into the list of integers a model reads. tokenizers runs that conversion in four stages. Normalization applies operations such as lowercasing or Unicode normalization to the raw text. Pre-tokenization splits the text into smaller pieces called pre-tokens. The model turns each pre-token into tokens and maps them to IDs in its vocabulary. Post-processing adds any special tokens the model expects.

The model stage is where most of the work described here happens. Eight of the ten model families measured in this article use byte pair encoding, or BPE. BPE starts from the bytes of a pre-token and repeatedly joins the highest ranked adjacent pair until no ranked pair remains. The ranking is learned when the tokenizer is trained and ships with it, so the same text always produces the same IDs. A merge never crosses a pre-token boundary. The other two families use WordPiece and Unigram, the two other model types the library supports.

The tokenization pipeline page documents the four stages. Tokenization algorithms documents BPE, WordPiece and Unigram.

Each stage was worked on. These are the changes that mattered:

BPE models use a regular expression to split the input text into smaller, easier to process chunks called pre-tokens. Merges happen inside a pre-token and never across the boundary between two of them, so this split decides what the rest of the pipeline sees.

That regular expression is a fixed parameter of the model. It ships with the tokenizer and never changes at runtime, so there is no need for a general-purpose regex engine to interpret it on every encode. An equivalent splitting function can be written by hand, once, for the pattern a given model actually uses.

A hand-written function can then use the SIMD instructions (single instruction, multiple data) of a modern CPU, which apply one operation to many bytes at once and suit UTF-8 text well. bitcannon views the input's bytes as parallel streams of bits, so boundaries fall out of boolean operations across whole registers instead of a scan that advances one character at a time. It decides 64 bytes per register operation. The same idea drives Parabix for text processing and simdjson for JSON.

This depends on recognising the pattern. A handful of grammars cover most byte-level BPE models, and a tokenizer whose pattern is not among them keeps the regex path and none of this speed-up. That is why the gains above vary as much as they do.

Real text contains many repeated words. Because BPE always produces the same token IDs for a given pre-token, v1 can save the result after processing it once. A thread-local cache maps each pre-token's bytes to its token IDs, allowing later occurrences to skip the merge process.

Naturally, as the input grows, the number of unique words can grow more slowly than the total number of words. Repeated words then account for an increasing share of the input. New words still appear, which accounts for the occasional misses in the animation below.

Caching works best when the input contains repeated pre-tokens. Input with few repeated pre-tokens can pay for lookups without receiving many hits.

The next major cost comes from the BPE merge loop. For each pre-token, the loop repeatedly finds the highest-priority adjacent pair and merges it. The previous implementation allocated new memory for every call and built a new priority queue for every pre-token.

v1 reuses a scratch buffer owned by the caller, removing those repeated allocations. It stores symbols in a flat array and links adjacent symbols by their positions in that array, which makes updates during merging cheaper. It also processes a batch of pre-tokens in a single model call.

Each candidate pair is also packed into a single 64-bit value, with the merge rank in the high bits. Comparing two candidates is then just comparing two integers, and "no merge here" is the largest possible value, so the loop finds its next merge without a branch.

Small differences in benchmark design can produce large differences in tokenizer performance. We used the following rules to keep the comparison consistent across engines.

Repeatedly encoding one document can be faster than encoding a stream of distinct documents on the same build. The first approach measures performance when the entire document is already represented in the cache. The second measures performance on new input while allowing previously seen pre-tokens to remain cached.

Both conditions are sometimes described as "warm," even though they measure different workloads. Our headline results use distinct documents, and the complete corpus is too large to fit in the cache. Tokenizer benchmarks should identify which workload they use because the choice can dominate the result.

Across the ten model families v1's encode path covers, it encodes text 3 to 30 times faster than v0.23 with one thread on an Apple M4 Max. The low end is t5-base, the high end gpt2. It scales at 76% of linear across eight workers. Throughout these changes, v1 produces exactly the same token IDs as the released library.

The overall improvement comes from several changes working together: a hand-written splitter in place of a regex engine, a cache that answers a repeated word without merging it again, a merge loop that never touches the allocator, and one model call per batch of pre-tokens instead of one per pre-token. Each reduces the work done at a different point in the pipeline.

The next priority is support for more model families. We will move additional models onto the new merge loop before 1.0.0. Once the release candidates stabilize, the next step will be bringing about the improvements within the transformers library and the rest of the ecosystem which depend on the tokenizers library.

This post is generated from tokbench results and will be updated as support expands.

A release candidate for v1 is on crates.io. The API you call is the one you already call, so the only thing that changes is which build you install.

Training is behind a default-on feature that pulls a C++ dependency with it. If you only need to encode, turn it off to exclude the training implementation:

Encoding is unchanged: same call, same ids.

Every figure in this post was measured against this crate. The Python bindings wrap the same code and are built from bindings/python, but they add per-call overhead that none of these measurements include.

The benchmarks in this post cover the completed release-candidate work listed first. The remaining sections show what is still required for 1.0.0 and what we plan to explore afterward.

#10021. AI boom threatens circuit board crunch to rival pandemic-era chip shortage

Trade body warns automotive, medical, and defense orders are being crowded out, with relief unlikely before mid-2028

The electronics industry faces a printed circuit board (PCB) shortage that could rival the pandemic-era chip crunch – with AI once again accused of hogging supplies.

The Global Electronics Association says demand is arriving "at a scale the supply chain was not built for," straining everything from glass fabric and resin to finished boards.

Its report, "The PCB Squeeze: A Wake-Up Call for Global Electronics," says AI servers need increasingly complex boards. While a typical PC board has about 12 layers of tracks, AI server boards can have 40 to 60 layers or more, and each additional layer requires more resin, copper foil, and laminate.

The supply of materials is set to be constrained through at least the first half of 2027, the report says, with meaningful relief unlikely before mid-2028.

Programs to deliver PCBs for automotive, industrial, medical and even the defense industries are being crowded out as AI soaks up scarce capacity, it claims.

The association's North American figures show orders growing much faster than deliveries. PCB bookings rose 56.1 percent in the first nine months of 2026 compared with the same period last year, while PCB shipments increased 13.3 percent.

Fabrication capacity is expanding, aimed at meeting the increased demand from the AI infrastructure sector, especially in Asia, where more than 90 percent of the world's boards are made. The report says that $10 billion has gone toward new PCB plants in Southeast Asia, and at least as much has been invested in China over the past three years, but the raw materials are themselves constrained.

It warns of lengthening lead times for those raw materials. Standard FR-4 laminate now takes six to eight weeks to ship, up from two to three weeks a year ago, while advanced low-loss laminates now take 14 to 18 weeks for delivery, for example.

Tightening supplies usually lead to price increases, and the report says that suppliers raised laminate costs by 30 percent in September, and that the price tag of some types of E-glass cloth for circuit boards has risen by 300 percent.

The report also puts copper prices up 37 percent over the past year. Concerns have been raised about copper supplies before, as The Register has reported multiple times.

The association compares the risk with the 2021 chip shortage, when disrupted supplies left manufacturers unable to secure even relatively mundane components.

New capacity is coming, but it is late and comes in dribs and drabs, according to the report, while AI demand just keeps on absorbing it as soon as it arrives.

The association's advice is for buyers to plan early, and to share realistic forecasts with suppliers rather than double-booking. Board makers should qualify alternative suppliers of materials such as laminate and copper foil before shortages bite, but it warns against stockpiling beyond real need, which adds to forward-buying pressure.

But it would like governments to step in, of course, by tracking board and material lead times with industry and offering tax incentives for investment in advanced PCB and substrate manufacturing equipment.

The wish list also includes state investment in research and development plus qualification of new alternative materials. It would like to see loan guarantees and grants to protect critical programs and small fabricators, structured so as to sustain new capacity if forward buying unravels and demand corrects in 2027.

"Yes, we are seeing constraint in upstream materials and have been reporting it for the past couple of quarters," said Cori Masters, senior research analyst director for Supply Chain Operations at Gartner.

"In addition, AI datacenter infrastructure build out is moving capacity support to high-layer count PCBs which increase throughput time and decreases availability of line utilization for more traditional PCB products," she told The Register. ®

#10019. Jun Kim, oMLX creator and maintainer, joins Hugging Face to support the MLX community

We are super excited to welcome Jun as our newest team member 🔥. We are completely invested in local AI, and MLX is a central piece of the ecosystem. We are delighted that Jun chose us to set up home and continue contributing to MLX.

MLX is Apple's framework for local AI, especially optimized for Apple Silicon. We are big MLX supporters since it was the Christmas present from Awni and Angelos in 2023, and proud that Hugging Face is the Hub where people find MLX models and contribute their own. Usage of open, local AI is accelerating, and we believe in a healthy ecosystem where people can find the tools that work for them.

Stability, and hopefully faster development! Graduating from a side job to a fully maintained and funded project will allow Jun to better guide the contributors and build for the long-term. oMLX stays Apache 2.0, and Jun keeps leading it as before.

Our end goal is to unblock the community to run local AI in any shape or form, and provide the tools and building blocks to make that happen. We expect oMLX to serve as a testbed for new ideas, while leveraging the foundational work of the dependencies it already relies upon, such as mlx-lm or mlx-vlm. We believe that strong modeling and inference libraries help the community, so we'd love to upstream work to wherever it makes sense. We have been collaborating with many projects mlx-lm, mlx-vlm, LMStudio, and we hope we can strengthen the relationship with Cheng, Prince, Yagil, and their teams to better serve the community together.

Concretely, one focus area is the quick transition from a transformers model definition to a reference MLX implementation that can be consumed by different engines, so each one can focus on the unique features they provide. The transformers library has become the reference for ML model definitions, we want to streamline the process to make new transformers models run on MLX.

We are incredibly excited about the future.

#10018. Transformers now runs llama.cpp quants

We're adding support for running GGUF models efficiently in transformers, so you can use checkpoints sized for your laptop's memory through the familiar transformers APIs. Pick a GGUF from the Hub, load it with from_pretrained, and start generating on your own machine.

Running AI models on your laptop has become much easier, and llama.cpp has been a big part of that. Its inference engine powers local AI tools such as Ollama, LM Studio, and Jan. Alongside projects like MLX, it has helped make local inference a practical option for everyday use.

A recent example of what local AI can feel like:

This is where we are right now. And i’m not gonna lie it feels pretty magical 🧙‍♀️Qwen3.6 27B running inside of Pi coding agent via Llama.cpp on the MacBook ProFor non-trivial tasks on the @huggingface codebases, this feels very, very close to hitting the latest Opus in Claude… pic.twitter.com/lsIxLoUneU

GGUF, developed by the llama.cpp team, is a widely used format for local inference. The team also shares quantized checkpoints under ggml-org on the Hub. Publishers such as Unsloth, LM Studio Community, and bartowski also provide ready-to-use GGUF checkpoints in a range of quantizations, so users can pick the version that fits their machine. GGUF models have been downloaded millions of times.

We want to make it easier to run these models locally with transformers, too. Compatibility is only useful if the model is pleasant to run. To bring performance close to llama.cpp, we're reusing its underlying ggml kernels through the kernels library, and reducing overhead in generate. Our initial focus is local inference on Apple Silicon, starting with the Qwen3.5 architecture.

GGUF packages model weights and metadata, including tokenizer information and an optional chat template, in one file. It supports different quantization levels, letting you trade some precision for a smaller memory footprint. Variants such as Q4_K_M mix tensor precisions, using mostly 4-bit weights while keeping sensitive tensors at higher precision.

Here's how quantization changes the file size of Unsloth's Qwen3.5-4B:

We suggest starting with Q4_K_M, then trying Q5_K_M or Q6_K if you have more memory available. More aggressive quantization can help larger models fit, but the quality tradeoff depends on the model and the task. Evaluate it on the work you actually want the model to do. The Hub's GGUF documentation describes the available quantization types.

To load a GGUF model, pass its Hub model_id and filename as gguf_file to from_pretrained.

No extra configuration is needed: when the weights stay packed on Metal, transformers automatically loads the compatible ggml/Metal layer kernels and uses ggml-org/ggml-attn as the attention implementation. If that kernel cannot be fetched, the model falls back to "sdpa" with a warning, and you can always force "sdpa" by passing attn_implementation="sdpa" explicitly. See the GGUF documentation for more loading options.

That is the only GGUF-specific step. Everything after it is the standard transformers API:

Without a compatible quantization kernel, the loader falls back to dequantizing the model and uses more memory.

You can also use the same checkpoint with transformers serve, which exposes an OpenAI-compatible API:

The model argument uses :.gguf: before the colon is the Hub repository (unsloth/Qwen3.5-4B-GGUF), and after it is the file to load (Qwen3.5-4B-Q4_K_M.gguf). This selects a specific quantization from a repository that may contain several.

For models whose chat template supports thinking, add --reasoning off to skip it or --reasoning on to enable it. The default, --reasoning auto, follows the chat template’s default. See the reasoning options for details.

You can connect a client such as Jan or Pi by adding a custom OpenAI-compatible provider with these settings:

transformers runs the model on your Mac, while the client provides the conversation interface. The same endpoint can be used by other clients that support this API.

Our reference for local inference performance is llama.cpp. The comparison below focuses on three GGUF checkpoints: a small dense model, a larger dense model, and a mixture-of-experts model.

The llama.cpp column comes from the llama-bench tool (build 5f55650a7, release b10200, Metal backend from ggml 0.18.0), run as llama-bench -m -p 0 -n 128 -r 3, which reports tg128: the token-generation rate over 128 decoded tokens, averaged across three repetitions, with prompt processing excluded. The transformers column is generate producing the same 128 tokens from a 12-token prompt, best of three warmed runs, and it includes prefill.

Measured on a MacBook Pro M2 Max, 32 GB unified memory, macOS 26.6, PyTorch 2.12.1, kernels 0.17.0, plugged in.

Transformers is close to llama.cpp across all three checkpoints. The chart uses the same measurements described above; it does not imply identical benchmark conditions, since the Transformers measurement includes prefill while llama-bench reports decode-only throughput.

When GGML and llama.cpp joined Hugging Face, we described their complementary roles: llama.cpp provides a foundation for local inference, while transformers provides a foundation for model definition. GGUF support brings those two closer together.

llama.cpp remains our recommended engine when your priority is efficient local inference. Its dedicated runtime, memory management, and broad hardware support are built around that goal. This integration gives developers a convenient way to work with the same GGUF checkpoints inside transformers:

For that last case, use GgufConfig(dequantize=True):

The bigger opportunity is bringing ggml's performance to models that llama.cpp does not support.

transformers already provides the PyTorch implementations of these architectures. With ggml kernels and quantization schemes available in PyTorch, we can work toward accelerating their supported operations without first implementing the entire model in llama.cpp. This is especially useful for new architectures, research models, and custom variants that may never receive a dedicated llama.cpp implementation.

That opportunity extends beyond the GGUF format itself. A kernel operates on tensors; it does not require the whole model to come from a GGUF file. The same building blocks can be integrated into other transformers models and loading workflows. This also opens a path to other modalities: computer vision models, audio models, and multimodal models could reuse compatible attention, normalization, and matrix multiplication kernels without first having a full implementation in llama.cpp. Each architecture still needs integration and validation; the initial GGUF examples here cover text generation.

We also wanted to show how far we can get while keeping the model and generation loop in Python. With the right kernels and an efficient generation loop, Python and PyTorch can deliver strong local inference performance. The kernels handle the heavy computation, while the generation loop keeps the GPU busy by avoiding unnecessary synchronization.

Our focus was to make eager execution fast without requiring torch.compile. For interactive use, we wanted a quick start and a steady stream of tokens, without compilation pauses or recompilation when input shapes change. The two main pieces of that work are the kernels and generate itself.

A kernel is a small program that performs an operation on the GPU. PyTorch supplies general-purpose implementations; a specialized kernel can do less work, combine several operations, or read quantized weights directly in their stored format.

The kernels library lets us distribute compatible builds of ggml's Metal kernels on the Hub and call them from transformers. That brings ggml's work into the PyTorch model without replacing the model with a separate inference runtime.

The first four packages build on ggml's kernels; the top-k kernel addresses a separate bottleneck in MoE routing. Together they reduce the GPU work needed for each generated token.

To show the contribution of the layer kernels, we compare the same packed GGUF checkpoints with and without them. The quantization kernel stays enabled in both configurations: disabling it would also change how weights are represented and would measure a different tradeoff.

Faster kernels only help if the GPU has work to do. During generation, the CPU schedules GPU operations and controls the loop that produces the next token. Reading a result back from the GPU can force the CPU to wait until queued operations finish. Repeating even a small wait for every token can noticeably reduce throughput.

Two changes address this in generate, which results in improvements for all transformers models (not just when running GGUF files):

These changes improve the generation loop around the model, so their usefulness extends beyond GGUF. They complement the kernel work: kernels reduce the cost of an operation, while fewer synchronization points let CPU scheduling and GPU execution overlap.

These measurements keep all layer kernels enabled; the bars isolate the changes to the generation loop.

The initial target is a single interactive conversation on Apple Silicon. There are a few boundaries to keep in mind:

If you have a GGUF model you would like to use in transformers, open an issue with the checkpoint and your use case. That will help us prioritize support for the models people are running locally.

We would like to thank Arthur Zucker for initiating this work and reviewing all of my PRs, and Cyril Vallez for the generate PRs. We are grateful to Sayak Paul, the llama.cpp team, and Bertrand Chevalier for their help integrating the kernels. We also thank Aritra Roy Gosthipaty and Pedro Cuenca for reviewing this blog post, and Lysandre Debut for overseeing the project.

#10017. Dutch data watchdog highlights safety issues with AI glasses

Devices found to misinterpret medication instructions and other scenarios impacting human safety

The Dutch Data Protection Authority (AP) has officially advised consumers against buying AI-powered smart glasses after safety tests revealed concerning behaviors beyond their controversial recording capabilities.

The AP recently tested six different models of smart glasses and found glaring issues, including a willingness to display dating advice to an adult glasses-wearer who expressed an interest in a minor.

In another case involving a cardiopulmonary resuscitation (CPR) simulation, testers noted that one pair of glasses informed the wearer that emergency services had been called and were scheduled to arrive at the scene, despite no one having made the call.

Some glasses did not properly process safety warnings on children’s toys, others made mistakes when reading medication leaflets, and some misinterpreted warnings for extreme weather events.

The AP did not specify the models it tested, saying only that they tested six models ranging from under €100 ($110) to over €500 ($550), including two that "were extensively tested in simulated real-life situations where human safety played a key role."

A spokesperson also declined to match any specific behavior to a model by price point (minor dating advice linked to a €354 pair of glasses, for example), adding that the research was intended to highlight the risks of AI glasses in a broader sense.

"Glasses that film you unnoticed are already concerning. Glasses that also give you incorrect advice when someone's life is at stake go a step too far," said Monique Verdier, vice chair at the AP.

"AI offers many opportunities, but we must be able to trust that technology. With the camera glasses examined, that trust cannot currently be justified."

The same warning mentioned the potential risks regarding data processing under the GDPR, as well as those related to the training of AI.

The AP doubled down on these earlier criticisms, saying the latest tests showed that the AI functions rely on processing data using servers mostly located outside of the European Union. Relatedly, it found that users were not given sufficient information about how the AI was processing the data they captured.

On a cybersecurity note, the tests threw up a range of issues, including the ability for people nearby the glasses-wearer to connect to the device without permission, view recordings, and in some cases operate the camera.

Further, the regulator echoed the pre-existing concerns about smart specs - those that helped give them their colloquial name “pervert glasses.”

Its tests found that with "virtually all of the camera glasses examined," the recording lights that are supposed to clearly show when a user is recording were dim and easily coverable.

The AP said that models could also be wangled into recording even when that light indicator was covered, which goes against what manufacturers so often claim.

"As a result, bystanders can barely see whether they are being filmed," it said.

The technology has a number of beneficial use cases, such as assisting the visually impaired, those with lower literacy levels, or for any number of other scenarios where people need help understanding the world around them

However, the watchdog's official stance on the technology, as it is today, deems smart glasses "unsafe… due to the risks to users and bystanders."

Verdier said politicians in the Netherlands and across Europe should take note of the results when developing AI policy.

"It is important that we, as a society, learn to deal with these types of high-risk AI products," she said.

"Simply banning everything provides some leeway in the beginning, but we cannot sustain that indefinitely. It is important that we collectively work on awareness, resilience, and ethical conscience."

When DEF CON announced a no pervert glasses policy ahead of its event in August, the move was broadly welcomed by attendees.

"Love to see a ‘no pervert glasses’ policy at DEF CON," said Eva Galperin, EFF director of cybersecurity, at the time.

Several other organizations have implemented similar restrictions, including Monopoly Events, which manages UK Comic Cons, national treasure pub chain Wetherspoons, and even Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE).

Like it or not, it's generally understood that a smartphone is usually recording something - or someone - at any given time, especially in urban areas.

On paper, the fact that smart glasses can record in public spaces isn’t wildly different from what’s already come to be expected from smartphones.

However, given how similar they appear to analog glasses and the ability to cover the recording light, it makes the act of public recording via glasses far more surreptitious, and thus concerning.

With smartphones, it's easy to see from the user's body language - holding the phone out in front of them - that they are recording. There are no overt signals displayed by wearers of smart glasses during image or video capture, which fuels a sense of unease about the technology in general.

A joint investigation by The Observer and BBC Radio 4 recently revealed how AI-enabled glasses went undetected through the airport-style security scanners used in the UK parliament.

The two news outlets found that a £60 ($78) pair of Chinese-made glasses bypassed the scanners and could be used to read upside-down documents on MPs' desks, recording data such as phone numbers and addresses to be accessed at a later point. ®
