#9862. Russia's Cold Relic APT Turns One Cloud Breach Into Another

The state-sponsored threat group is using data stolen from one victim to target others via convincing impersonations and social engineering attacks.

The Russian cyber-espionage group known as Cold Relic is turning cloud breaches into a springboard for targeting a victim organization's wider network of trusted relationships.

It's a tactic that researchers at Google Threat Intelligence Group (GTIG) observed the attacker deploy with clinical efficiency in two separate compromises involving US organizations over the past year.

In the first intrusion, late last year, the attackers gained control of a cloud administrator account and harvested internal communications, employee details, and other organizational records. Cold Relic actors later used that material to impersonate an employee of the first organization for a successful social engineering attack on an individual at a second organization.

The activity, GTIG researchers said, shows how traditional social engineering is becoming more closely tied to attacks on cloud identities. Once inside an organization's cloud environment, an attacker can gather the kind of internal information that makes a message from a supposedly trusted colleague or business contact much harder to spot as a scam.

Related:China's 'Armory Castle' Lays Siege to VMware vCenter Zero-Day

The campaigns "demonstrate the convergence of human-centric social engineering and cloud identity abuse," GTIG researchers wrote in a blog post. "By obtaining access to strategic personnel rosters and operational documents, Russian intelligence services turn legitimate business communications into attack vectors against trusted partners."

Cold Relic (also known as Star Blizzard, Callisto, and Gossamer Bear) is a cyber-espionage group that Google researchers have been tracking — and disrupting — since 2015. The US government has assessed the outfit as working within Russia's Federal Security Service (FSB) and tasked with collecting information of political and strategic interest to Moscow.

Though low-profile, Cold Relic has notched up numerous high-value targets including defense contractors, government officials, and NGOs across North America and Europe. One of its favorite post-compromise activities, according to GTIG, is to steal emails and data that can help it establish "authentic pretexts" and convincing impersonations when reaching out to other potential targets.

In the first intrusion in late 2025, Cold Relic used stolen credentials for a super admin account to access a US organization's cloud environment. The attackers routed their activity through a residential proxy located near the organization, so their connections appeared to originate from a familiar geographic area. The attacker repeatedly kept sending the actual account holder multifactor authentication (MFA) push notifications until the overwhelmed user approved one.

Related:Second Norwegian Energy Company Breached in 2 Days

After gaining access, Cold Relic actors registered their own device on the network and established additional ways to authenticate to it, including via passkeys, backup MFA codes, and additional rogue MFA devices. The threat group used the stolen Super Admin user privileges to exfiltrate the organization's cloud storage, including full employee lists, email conversations, and organizational directories and contact lists. The threat actors then initiated several anti-forensics measures that allowed it to maintain access to the compromised network for several months.

In the second attack, earlier this year, Cold Relic impersonated an employee of the first company to contact an individual at a second organization through an encrypted messaging app. The threat actors sent the unsuspecting target phishing links disguised as documents relevant to their ongoing conversation.

After stealing the victim's Microsoft Entra ID credentials and authentication tokens, Cold Relic used them to access the organization's Google Workspace environment through its federated single sign-on system. The attackers then helped themselves to files from the compromised user's cloud drive while also seeking out email archives, chat records, credentials, personnel information, and other data of potential intelligence value.

Related:China-Nexus Actors Breach 10 Organizations in AI-Driven Attacks

"Cold Relic is highly adept at leveraging social networks and impersonation of key individuals to achieve a realistic pretense for reaching out to the targeted individual or organization," Wes Shields, security engineer at GTIG, tells Dark Reading. "Once they have achieved their initial access goal, they move quickly to maintain persistence and exfiltrate data."

The lesson for organizations is to train employees to be wary of unexpected messages, particularly when they arrive through communication channels a supposed colleague or business contact doesn't normally use. If a message seems unusual, employees should verify the sender's identity through a separate, previously established channel before responding or acting on it, Shields advises.

"In today's hyper-connected world, it is impossible to have employees not be reachable via multiple channels, and attackers are taking advantage of this," he says.

Joseph Spero, principal incident response consultant at Google, recommends other measures to limit the damage from identity-based attacks. These include enforcing phishing-resistant MFA, restricting and auditing passkey registrations, hardening MFA registration procedures, and auditing OAuth grants.

"Short-lived sessions and the principle of least privilege will limit the potential scope of access when credentials are compromised," he says. "When a compromise is suspected, mandate session revocation in addition to resetting passwords and MFA mechanisms."

Illinois-based Jai Vijayan is a veteran, award-winning technology journalist with more than 25 years of experience covering cybersecurity. His information security reporting has explored everything from ransomware, nation-state threats, and identity security to AI risk, critical infrastructure protection, software supply chain security, cloud security and emerging enterprise technologies.

Over the course of his career, Jai has written news stories, feature articles, survey reports, white papers, and e-books for enterprise and technology audiences. He has also moderated panel discussions and executive roundtables featuring CISOs, security researchers, and industry leaders.

His work has earned multiple industry honors, including a Joint ASBPE Excellence Award for Best Coverage of Government IT, and a Joint Jesse H. Neal Award for wireless LAN security coverage. Jai holds a Master’s degree in statistics from Bangalore University, and studied broadcasting and electronic communication at Marquette University in Milwaukee.

#9861. The Definitive Fine-Tuning Guide for 3D Generation Models

TLDR; In this blog, we provide fine-tuning scripts and containers to fine-tune TRELLIS.2, a popular 3D model on your 3D assets, that can run both locally and on Hugging Face Jobs. If you are interested in fine-tuning, you can use our scripts with few arguments (assuming you updated your dataset to Hugging Face Hub) or tinker with them yourself with this repository. If you want to learn more, we go through how the script works. Let’s go!

3D generation has many uses in robotics, simulation, media, and entertainment. In these fields, it is difficult to make generated objects obey strict rules and standardize model and data representations. There are many file formats, such as GLB and PLY. There are also many representations, such as neural radiance fields (NeRFs) and 3D Gaussian splatting (3DGS). Each one has different advantages and disadvantages.

TRELLIS introduced a common internal representation, called a unified latent representation. Its decoders convert this representation into 3D models in the required output format. Thus, you do not have to use different models for each representation format.

The same team then released TRELLIS.2, which improves the model's representation of 3D structure. But neither model gives an easy way to adapt it to a specific task.

A general-purpose model, such as TRELLIS.2, can make errors in details that are important for a specific application. For example, a user may need accurate geometry for furniture models. Without fine-tuning for that task, the pretrained model can produce geometry that is insufficiently accurate. We use a subset of GSO that has 188 footwear objects for our experiment. In our initial tests, the pretrained model usually produced shoes that looked correct, but the soles were incorrect. We test whether a LoRA can make the soles more accurate.

Our goal is to use the Google Scanned Objects (GSO) dataset to improve the performance of TRELLIS.2 on a specific object category. We will explain which pipeline components to fine-tune and which to leave unchanged during training. The pipeline separates structure, detailed geometry, and materials. Thus, we will fine-tune only the components that are important for our task.

Choosing what to freeze matters as much as choosing what to fine-tune.

LoRA, short for low-rank adaptation, fine-tunes a model by training small adapter matrices while keeping the original weights frozen. This reduces the number of trainable parameters and the memory needed for their gradients and optimizer state. We use Hugging Face’s PEFT library to add and train these adapters. For more information, read our LoRA guide.

Hugging Face Jobs runs containerized workloads on cloud hardware. We use it for preprocessing and for training. To use your own GPU instead, see the local Docker commands below. Before you start, make sure that you have:

Before we train, let’s look at how TRELLIS.2 generates a 3D object and where we’ll add LoRA adapters.

TRELLIS.2 has five main stages: remove the image background, encode the image, predict the coarse structure, generate detailed geometry, and generate materials. The pipeline then exports the result as a textured mesh.

First, BiRefNet removes the background from the input image. DINOv3-L then encodes the image into feature tokens. The generation models use these tokens to guide the 3D object.

The sparse-structure flow DiT predicts the object's coarse shape. It is a diffusion transformer (DiT) that makes a small latent of size 16³ × 8. A variational autoencoder (VAE) decoder then changes this latent into a 64 × 64 × 64 occupancy grid. Each voxel in the grid shows if that location is part of the object. A voxel is a pixel in three dimensions. We add LoRA adapters to this model because its output guides the geometry stage.

O-Voxel is the 3D format of TRELLIS.2. It is a sparse voxel grid. It keeps only the voxels on the object's surface. Each voxel keeps local geometry, such as a mesh vertex, and material attributes. Because the format is small, a CPU changes a mesh into O-Voxel in seconds. A GPU changes O-Voxel back into a mesh in seconds.

Structured sparse latents come from TRELLIS. They keep 3D data in sparse tensors, which makes computation faster. The model uses only approximately 10% of the voxels in the grid, so it does not spend compute on empty voxels. Thus, the shape flow DiT and the texture flow DiT are sparse transformers. The sparse-structure flow DiT is a dense transformer.

The shape flow DiT uses the occupancy grid and the DINOv3 feature tokens to make a latent. Another VAE decoder then changes this latent into O-Voxel geometry at a resolution of 512 × 512 × 512.

We add LoRA adapters to the DiT at this stage because it controls the object's shape.

In the last stage, the texture flow DiT uses the shape latent and the DINOv3 features as input. It defines the materials and textures of the geometry's surface. A VAE decoder then changes the latent into base color, metallic, roughness, and alpha values for each voxel. We do not add LoRA adapters to this stage. Our dataset has diffuse color maps, but it lacks the separate material maps this stage needs for training. Also, our problem is the shoe's shape. The base model already makes good colors and textures.

Finally, the pipeline combines the geometry and material attributes into a textured mesh and exports it as a GLB file.

We add LoRA adapters only to the sparse-structure flow DiT and the shape flow DiT. These DiTs control the object's shape and geometry. We freeze the texture flow DiT to keep its current capabilities.

Our dataset contains diffuse color maps that include baked lighting effects. To train the texture flow DiT, we need separate material maps. The color maps in our dataset mix surface color with lighting. Thus, they are not correct targets for this training.

If we train the texture flow DiT on these maps, it can learn to show lighting as a surface property. It can also forget what it learned before, a problem called catastrophic forgetting.

Our subset has 188 shoes from the 1,030 objects in GSO. For a dataset this small, LoRA is a better choice than full fine-tuning. Full fine-tuning costs much more. It can also overwrite what the model already does well (its learned priors). Our configuration trains approximately 9.3 million adapter parameters in total for both targeted DiTs. We use rank 8 adapters in the attention and feed-forward (MLP) layers of the sparse-structure flow DiT. We use rank 16 adapters in the attention layers of the shape flow DiT. The rank sets the size of the adapter matrices. A higher rank lets the adapter learn more.

A 3D model setup can need many dependencies and installation steps. We supply two Docker images (that you can run on Jobs or your own machine) with the necessary software. One image is for preprocessing, and one is for fine-tuning.

To train your LoRA adapters and upload them to the Hub:

Then we explain the fine-tuning script, its settings, and how each setting affects training.

We’ll walk through three parts of the experiment:

We save the preprocessed dataset so that all training runs can reuse it.

The preprocessing container uses Blender to render 16 views of each object. LoRA training will use these views as conditioning images. Blender runs without a display, through the xvfb-run utility. The container also processes each object through the preprocessing pipeline. See the footwear dataset here for an example intermediate output. For our 188 objects, the full run took approximately 1 hour on an a100-large job. A compact version of the preprocessing pipeline is also available in this companion repository.

For Hugging Face Jobs, we pass the following arguments:

This container accepts a few more arguments (regardless of being run on Hugging Face Jobs or with Docker), that you can find documented over here. The steps taken in the preprocessing pipeline are documented in this section later.

The training container loads the prepared dataset and a configuration preset or file. It records training metrics with Trackio. Use the Trackio dashboard to monitor the run.

We use ‘ss’ and ‘shape’ to indicate the two modes we have for training the LoRAs. The ‘ss’ mode will finetune only the Sparse-Structure Flow DiT, whereas the ‘shape’ mode will finetune the Shape Flow DiT. Under the hood, they simply reference different config.json files to use for each stage. More details about the process is available in this section later.

If you set --push-to, the container uploads adapter checkpoints to the Hub. The container accepts parameters that are also documented here for brevity. A compact script is also available in the same repository.

If you want to play around and fine-tune with the already-processed dataset we have, feel free to use the following set of commands.

The commands and flags are the same as for Hugging Face Jobs. Only the Docker options are different.

If you want to use our already-preprocessed dataset locally on your machine of choice, use the following commands:

Our trained LoRA adapters are in this repository: suvadityamuk/trellis-2-finetune-gso

We use TRELLIS.2’s frozen encoders to convert the input meshes into training latents. We save these latents, so later runs do not have to encode the meshes again.

We also render 16 views of each object in Blender. During training, we select one random view for each sample as the conditioning image. We keep 9 of the 188 objects for evaluation and train on the other 179. These held-out objects show whether the adapters work on objects unseen by the model during training.

Some of the views that Blender rendered for one object

The first snippet sets up the data. FLOW selects the flow DiT to train (ss or shape), and STEPS sets the number of optimizer steps. A batch size of 4 with 4 gradient accumulation steps gives an effective batch size of 16. Then, the snippet loads the LoRA config file for the selected flow DiT, makes the dataset in the TRELLIS.2 format, removes the held-out objects, and makes the data loader for fine-tuning.

We use the peft library to insert LoRA adapters into the selected layers. TRELLIS.2 has a custom forward pass, so the standard PeftModel() wrapper does not work. Instead, we call inject_adapter_in_model(). This function adds the adapters directly to the model and keeps its custom interface.

We keep the trainable adapter weights in 32-bit floating point (fp32) for numerical stability and use bfloat16 (bf16) autocasting for the forward pass. Autocasting lets PyTorch use lower precision for some operations, which decreases memory use. Autocasting does not change how the frozen backbone weights are stored.

It’s important to note that our objective function here is good-old rectified flow matching (as seen in popular image-generation models like Stable Diffusion 3, Flux 2, and others). TRELLIS.2 used the same objective in pretraining, so it is a good choice for fine-tuning. For the theory, read this blog about flow matching.

We update only the LoRA parameters in the sparse-structure and shape DiTs. All original model weights remain frozen.

The snippets below show the core training loop for one stage. They are simpler than the container code and do not include some setup steps. For the full workflow, use the container commands.

We initialize the optimizer and load DINOv3 to extract features from the input images.

We then follow these steps within the training loop:

The training loop computes the loss and updates the adapter weights. Gradient accumulation adds the gradients from 4 small batches before each optimizer step. Gradient checkpointing saves GPU memory by recomputing some intermediate values during backpropagation. The outer loop runs for a given number of optimizer steps, whereas the inner loop accumulates gradients over a set of batches.

For each batch, DINOv3 encodes the conditioning image. For classifier-free guidance (CFG) dropout, the loop sets the conditioning to zero for a random fraction (p_uncond) of the samples. Then, it calculates the flow-matching loss with bf16 autocasting. After the inner loop, it clips the gradients to prevent very large updates and does an optimizer step. It logs the loss every 10 steps and saves an adapter checkpoint every 500 steps.

We trained two adapters: one for the sparse-structure DiT and one for the shape DiT. The LoRA config files in the container image contain the full training settings: ss_flow_lora_gso.json for the sparse-structure flow DiT and slat_flow_img2shape_lora_gso.json for the shape flow DiT. Each run used one A100 80 GB on Hugging Face Jobs. The sparse-structure run took 7.2 hours, and the shape run took 3.6 hours.

The training loss of the sparse-structure flow DiT falls quickly at the start, then more slowly. The loss of the shape flow DiT stays at approximately the same level. These curves show how the training objective changes, but they do not directly measure the quality of the generated geometry.

Flow-matching loss varies with the sampled objects, noise, and timesteps. To find out if fine-tuning improves the geometry, we must also compare outputs on the held-out objects.

The figure below compares outputs for five of the nine held-out objects. It shows the input image, the base model’s generated output, the base output after a rotation adjustment, the output with the footwear adapters, and the reference scan. In these examples, the soles from the fine-tuned model are closer to the scans.

We also use three metrics to evaluate the geometry on the test set:

In the chart’s nine-object comparison, the base model has a mean F-score of 0.276, compared with 0.803 for the model with the footwear adapters. Chamfer distance falls from 0.174 to 0.033, and normal consistency rises from 0.530 to 0.804. With both adapters, the F-score is better on all nine held-out objects.

For the statistics of all runs, see this Trackio space.

Phew, so there we go! We fine-tuned TRELLIS.2 for footwear generation by adding LoRA adapters to the two model components that control geometry. We prepared the data once, trained the adapters in separate jobs, and evaluated the outputs on held-out objects.

The main lesson is to select a training target that agrees with the problem and the data that you have. For this experiment, we fine-tuned the structure and shape stages and froze the texture stage.

Next, we can examine if the same choices help other 3D generation models, such as Pixal3D and UniLat3D.

Gaussian-splat and world-generation models, such as HunyuanWorld 2.0 and NVIDIA Lyra 2.0, are also possible next steps. Their representations and training pipelines can need different methods.

Thank you for following along, and see you in the next one! 👋🤗

#9860. Africa Retakes Top Spot as Most Attacked Region, Led by Nigeria Surge

Breaking cybersecurity news, news analysis, commentary, and other content from around the world, with an initial focus on the Middle East & Africa, the Asia Pacific, Europe, and Latin America.

Nigeria faced more than double the cyber threats of the previous year, with Angola and Kenya also in the top 5 most-attacked countries globally.

Organizations in Africa faced an average of 3,834 cyberattacks per week in October, a jump of 38% from a year earlier, making the continent the most-attacked region for the first time in more than a year.

Nigeria, Angola, and Kenya were among the top-five most targeted countries, with Nigeria topping the list with nearly 6,700 attacks targeting organizations in the country every week; that marks a 140% increase over October 2025, according to data published by Check Point Research earlier this month. The nations are among those rapidly pushing technological transformation of their infrastructure, expanding connectivity, investing in digital services, and putting sensitive data in network-connected applications and storage.

The fast transformation is exposing more opportunities for attackers, says Shayimamba Conco, chief technology officer and security evangelist in the Office of the CTO at Check Point Software.

Related:Chinese AI Project Scouts Spies in Taiwan Chip Industry

"All this rapid digital expansion is now happening within the region, but then, at the same time, this [expansion] is outpacing improvements in security maturity," he says, adding that security improvements are uneven across the continent. "Yes, some areas — let's say for example, South Africa — it's adopting cybersecurity at a much quicker rate than the rest of the Africa region, but there will be those regions which are still lagging behind a bit."

The significant increase in average weekly attacks pushed African organizations past those in Latin America as the favored targets of cyberattackers. In the first quarter of 2026, Latin America averaged more than 3,000 attacks per week, surpassing the approximate 2,700 attacks targeting African organizations. In September, the two regions essentially tied in terms of attacks, with Africa once again becoming the most popular target in October.

Globally, organizations experienced an average of 2,550 weekly cyberattacks in October, down 9% from September but up a third from the previous year. While Africa encountered the most weekly attacks, both Latin America and Asia-Pacific regions saw a greater-than-average number — 3,483 and 3,436, respectively.

Globally, cyberattacks focused heavily on the education sector, with the average academic institution suffering more than 5,900 attacks per week, up a third from the same month in 2025. The education sector has topped the global list of popular targets every month, with organizations made attractive to attackers because of their large data sets and reliance on legacy systems, says Conco.

Related:Malicious Linux Implants Mimic Asian Mail Security Products

"There is a lack of budget when it comes to not just IT, but specifically cybersecurity," he says. "A junior IT engineer has to manage these vast environments, which are hard to lock down by nature, because you've got all these students who need access to all these applications and resources."

In Africa, however, cyberattackers most often targeted financial services, government agencies, and the energy sector, according to Check Point's data.

The countries are racing to improve their cybersecurity postures and address persistent threats. Nigeria's National Information Technology Development Agency (NITDA) continues to work on the details of the nation's cybersecurity and cloud-sovereignty policies. Last month, Operation Serengeti 3.0 — a joint task force between Interpol and 20 African countries — led to the arrest of more than 1,500 suspects and the recovery of $105 million in stolen funds. In August, Operation Jackal IV targeted West African crime syndicates, leading to more than 200 arrests.

Check Point also flagged the use of AI in companies as a potential weak point, finding that about 2.9% of prompts to generative AI and large language models (LLMs) posed a high risk of leaking sensitive information. The risk is steadily increasing over time, from 2.3% in August to 2.5% in September.

Related:UAE, Saudi Arabia Face Onslaught of Increasingly Complex Cyberattacks

Interpol has also observed that attackers are increasingly using AI in a way that has impacted African nations. In its African Cybercrime Assessment Report 2026, Interpol found that 55% of reported cybercrimes across Africa used AI to some degree.

"Cybercrime has emerged as one of the most significant criminal threats to the region," Neal Jetton, Director of Interpol’s Cybercrime unit, said in a statement in August. "AI is automating every stage of a cyberattack from reconnaissance and phishing to extortion and evasion. However, we see that when countries work together, cybercriminal infrastructure can be identified, disrupted and dismantled."

#9859. We Tested Every REST Endpoint and Missed the Queue That Dropped $62K

Automation Architect & Lead SDET | Killing flaky tests and breaking pipeline bottlenecks.

Automation Architect & Lead SDET | Killing flaky tests and breaking pipeline bottlenecks.

Automation Architect & Lead SDET | Killing flaky tests and breaking pipeline bottlenecks.

That was the output of aws sqs get-queue-attributes on prod-merchant-payouts-dlq when our finance lead finally asked why Tuesday's Stripe Connect batch was missing $62,400 in disbursements.

Every single REST API contract test in our monorepo had passed that morning. Our Playwright suite was green. Our Go service's unit tests were green. Our TypeScript worker's unit tests were green.

None of them caught the bug, because the bug did not live on an HTTP route. It lived in the invisible gap between a Go service calling sqs.SendMessage and a Node.js worker calling JSON.parse(record.Body) as PayoutRequestedEvent.

Engineering teams spend huge amounts of energy locking down synchronous HTTP boundaries. We generate TypeScript clients from OpenAPI specs, run Supertest against Express routers, and fail CI if a response field changes from int to string.

Then we take an asynchronous SQS queue, a Kafka topic, or an internal SNS fan-out—which often carries the actual money-moving side effects—and treat it like a lawless JSON dropbox.

In our case, two separate teams owned the two ends of prod-merchant-payouts:

In payout-worker, the consumer had a type annotation that looked safe in code review and meant literally nothing at runtime:

When ledger-go refactored its decimal serialization to avoid float rounding and started emitting "payoutCents": "14900" as a string instead of 14900 as an integer, JSON.parse happily returned a string. Downstream, Math.round(payload.payoutCents) did not throw—Wait: actually, Math.round("14900") works in JavaScript!

What did throw was the strict Postgres BIGINT / Stripe SDK validation two functions later (Invalid integer: "14900.00" when a fractional fee was included), crashing the worker, exhausting maxReceiveCount: 3, and dumping 4,819 messages into prod-merchant-payouts-dlq.

Nobody was watching the DLQ metric in Datadog because that queue had sat at 0 for eight months.

When we pulled the two repos side-by-side after replaying the DLQ, both teams had written tests for that exact flow:

Static fixtures in consumer unit tests are a slow-acting poison. The day you write fixtures/payout-message.json, it matches reality. Six months later, after three producer refactors, your consumer tests are certifying a payload shape that no longer exists anywhere in production.

We did not want to deploy a heavy Confluent Schema Registry just for 14 SQS queues. We wanted something boring that worked across Go and TypeScript inside GitHub Actions with zero new infrastructure.

So we made JSON Schema (Draft 2020-12) the single source of truth inside a lightweight shared directory (contracts/queues/*.schema.json), paired with:

Here is contracts/queues/payout-requested.v1.schema.json:

And here is the TypeScript consumer boundary wrapper (src/queues/validateMessage.ts) that replaced JSON.parse(...) as ...:

Notice additionalProperties: false and "type": "integer" on payoutCents. If ledger-go ever serializes "14900" as a string again, parsePayoutMessage rejects it in under 0.1 milliseconds with an unmistakable SCHEMA_DRIFT_ERROR instead of letting it corrupt downstream state.

Validating a schema in memory is only half the story. You also want to prove that the Go producer's actual serialized bytes survive SQS attributes, base64/JSON encoding, and the TypeScript consumer's parsePayoutMessage() function.

We added a 55-line integration test (tests/contracts/sqs-payout-contract.test.ts) that spins up LocalStack via Testcontainers (or a GitHub Actions service container), runs the Go producer binary's emit-sample command to push real messages onto a local queue, and lets the TypeScript consumer pull and validate them:

That single test runs in 6.4 seconds in GitHub Actions. No mocked JSON fixtures. If a Go developer changes int64 to string on PayoutCents—even by adding ,string to a Go struct tag—that test blows up on their PR before payout-worker ever sees it in production.

The other embarrassing half of the $62K incident was not technical—it was operational. A queue had 4,819 failed payout messages sitting in it for 19 hours because nobody had wired an alarm to ApproximateNumberOfMessagesVisible > 0 on *-dlq.

We fixed that across all 14 queues in one Terraform module (infra/modules/sqs_dlq_alarm/main.tf) so every new queue gets a PagerDuty/Slack alert on message #1 in the DLQ, not message #4,819:

Zero tolerance on DLQ depth sounds aggressive until you realize a dead-letter queue is literally a bucket of failed customer promises. If one message lands there, you want to know within 60 seconds, not when finance reconciles Stripe payouts on Wednesday morning.

Putting a strict JSON Schema validator on a queue consumer introduces a subtle trap during rolling deployments: in-flight messages.

When Kubernetes rolls payout-worker to a new version, there can easily be 800 messages still sitting in SQS serialized by the previous version of ledger-go. If you rename a required field or tighten an enum in payout-requested.v1.schema.json, your new consumer pods will immediately reject valid in-flight messages as SCHEMA_DRIFT_ERROR.

We learned that the hard way on our second schema update. Now we enforce two rules in CI:

One last thing nobody tells you until you actually have to drain a 4,819-message financial DLQ: you cannot just click "Start DLQ Redrive" in the AWS Console and walk away.

During the 19-hour outage, our finance team had already manually wired payouts for 140 urgent enterprise merchants via the Stripe dashboard. If we had blindly redriven all 4,819 messages back into the main queue, those 140 merchants would have been paid twice.

Before replaying a single message, we added an INSERT INTO processed_queue_events (event_id) VALUES ($1) ON CONFLICT DO NOTHING idempotency guard backed by Postgres, pre-seeded it with the 140 manually settled eventIds, and ran a small redrive script that patched "payoutCents" from string to integer on the fly while logging every skipped duplicate.

We tested the redrive script with --dry-run on the first 50 DLQ messages, verified the Stripe idempotency keys matched, and then drained the remaining 4,769 messages in batches of 100. The whole replay finished in 4 minutes and 40 seconds across 20 concurrent workers, with zero double payouts and zero manual spreadsheet reconciliation afterward.

That idempotency table stayed in payout-worker permanently—because SQS is at-least-once delivery anyway, and sooner or later every distributed queue delivers the same message twice.

Once we put JSON Schema contracts and LocalStack round-trip tests on our SQS queues, we expected fewer production outages. And yes, we have had zero schema-drift DLQ incidents in the five months since.

What surprised me was how much faster onboarding got. New engineers stopped having to grep through three Go repositories to figure out what shape an SQS event actually had—they just opened contracts/queues/*.schema.json and read the exact contract in ten seconds.

If your test suite checks every REST route twice while your SQS, Kafka, or BullMQ workers still rely on JSON.parse(...) as MyType and hand-written test fixtures, you are only testing half your system. The other half is one struct tag away from a very quiet, very expensive pileup.

#9858. LLMON: An LLM-Native Markup Language, now in Granite 4.1 3B and 8B

LLMs rely on their context to generate the next set of tokens. Over a long trajectory, the context fills with numerous types of components: a system prompt, past conversation turns, instructions that act on retrieved documents, tool responses or user data, requirements constraining the allowed output, and reasoning chains. The context carries a rich structure, most of which is either implicit to the model or encoded in formats such as JSON that were not designed to be digested by LLMs. This is one of the main reasons LLMs, particularly those on the smaller end of the scale, are brittle and sometimes fail in unexpected ways. The lack of explicit structure can also be exploited by attackers, for example, in the form of prompt injections.

To address this, we developed LLMON (LLM Object Notation, pronounced “lemon”), an LLM-native markup language for explicitly communicating structure and semantics to the models. Semantically coherent components are marked with meaningful tags which are wrapped in reserved special-token delimiters. Data schemas, including nesting, are stated in a way that is unambiguous to a causal LLM. Unique IDs make it possible to point to specific instructions, which could reside anywhere in the context, and bind them to the data payloads they should act on, analogous to the way functions are called and arguments are passed to them in programming languages.

Today we are releasing two experimental preview models, derived from Granite 4.1 base models, trained to consume and generate LLMON-marked text: granite-4.1-3b-LLMON-preview and granite-4.1-8b-LLMON-preview. We are also releasing a GitHub repo, which includes a toolkit for working with LLMON and examples of workflows and templates.

JSON was designed for parsers, not for causal language models. The tokenizer is not constrained to respect the grammar, and structure is encoded by tokens ({, ", :) that may also appear in normal text. To a model, a quotation mark inside a document and a quotation mark that closes a field are the same token. Escaping rules that are clear to a parser are only statistical patterns to a model. Nesting depth is encoded by counting brackets, which transformers are known to be weak at, especially over long spans.

LLMON, on the other hand, is an XML-like markup whose structural delimiters are reserved special tokens rather than characters, so structure and content use separate parts of the vocabulary. Tags are stated at the beginning of each span, and the boundaries between spans are explicit. Nested structures are stated locally so the model does not need to keep track of the hierarchy over long spans.

Since most teams already have pipelines built around JSON, we created conversion tools and example notebooks that translate JSON to LLMON and back in a lossless manner.

LLMON does not replace chat templates; rather, it enriches them. Where regular chat templates tell the model which part belongs to which role (system, user, assistant), LLMON tells it what each component means and how components relate to each other, within and across roles.

The LLMON preview models ship with their own chat template, so you build the same messages list you would pass to any chat model and call apply_chat_template as usual; it renders the LLMON shown below. The only difference is that a turn can now name its parts and mark each one exec: True or False. A part marked True is bound into the exec block at the bottom of the rendered output, which states which instruction to run and what it operates on; a part marked False is still rendered into the context but is referenced by nothing.

Which the model receives as the following (with newlines and indentation added here for readability, as the template emits none):

The two-character block IDs are drawn from a fixed set that this tokenizer encodes as single tokens, so addressing a block always costs two tokens regardless of which ID is drawn.

The role is still a single user turn, but its components reach the model as five separate addressable blocks, bound together by a sixth (the exec block) that states: run this instruction, on this data, subject to these two requirements, and put the answer in the block named here, which is the same assistant block the model then fills. A conventional template would have flattened all components into one string and left the model to infer which part was the task, which was the subject, and which were constraints.

Indirect prompt injection is a type of attack where a malicious instruction is hidden in a data payload, such as a retrieved document, a tool response, or user-provided data. This is the problem LLMON’s instruction/data separation is designed to address.

We compared the LLMON previews against several open-source and closed-source models. We evaluated on the OPI benchmark, which places the injection in the data of classic NLP tasks. Several attack strategies are employed. We report robustness, defined as 1 − attack success rate: the share of attacks where the model does not carry out the injected instruction.

All non-LLMON models are highly susceptible, carrying out the injected instructions with high probability. LLMON practically eliminates the problem on this benchmark, avoiding 47% more attacks relative to the best frontier model that we tested, and 95% more than the best open-source model. We observe similar trends on other benchmarks (ASB and StruQ). It is worth noting that these benchmarks test robustness to static indirect prompt injections. The instruction/data separation directly addresses this type of attack. We are actively working on also improving adaptive attacks which unfold over many chat turns.

Safety gains don’t come at the expense of general capability. Across standard benchmark categories, the LLMON models perform on par with the Granite 4.1 Instruct models.

In short, if you’re experimenting with Granite 4.1 3B or 8B today, you can swap in the LLMON preview and should see comparable general performance with much stronger resistance to prompt injection. No conversion pipeline is required. Naming the turn's parts (e.g., instruction, data, requirement as in the example above) is enough. The shipped chat template turns those into LLMON blocks for you. Our LLMON-converters library goes one level deeper: if a part is itself structured, such as a JSON document, LLMONizing it preserves that structure as typed, individually addressable blocks, instead of one opaque string.

The models start from Granite 4.1 base checkpoints rather than the released instruct models, so LLMON behavior is learned during post-training rather than layered on an existing chat format.

LLMON defines six delimiters that mark the start and end of tags and allow nesting and anchoring; they are installed in the tokenizer as reserved single tokens. We re-serialized a conventional instruction-tuning corpus into LLMON: every prompt component becomes its own addressable block, and each turn carries an execution block naming which instruction to run, which inputs it operates on, and where the output goes. The task mix is the one a normal instruct model sees (chat, multi-turn, RAG, tool calling), which is why benchmark performance stays close to the conventionally tuned model. In addition, we augment the data with decoy instructions and data blocks that are present in context but deliberately left unbound, while the target output is unchanged. So the model learns to follow the dependencies dictated by the execution block and ignore the rest. Reinforcement learning follows: five sequential GRPO stages spanning multi-domain reasoning, RLHF, knowledge calibration, and math, followed by a final DPO stage on a thousand on-policy preference pairs built from the model’s own responses to injection attempts.

The resulting privilege rule falls out of this layout rather than an added guardrail: an instruction reached through an execution block is authoritative, while anything reached as input (data, documents, tool schemas, tool results) is material to read, not a command to follow. Furthermore, instructions and data spans that are not called on in the execution block are ignored. This is a learned behavior, not an enforced guarantee. To see how this plays out in the attention layers of a LLMON model, try the LLMON Attention Visualization on Hugging Face Spaces.

LLMON is not tied to a fixed schema: you can choose tag names and structure that fit your domain and fine-tune an adapter to read and write them. We demonstrate this on ScienceWorld, a text-based benchmark where an agent carries out elementary science tasks (such as boiling water) by issuing one command at a time and receiving a score from the simulator. We defined a vocabulary capturing the structure in the planning trajectories involved in solving these tasks. The vocabulary includes tags such as instr.task.goal, req.planning_policy.rule, data.state.room, data.state.inventory and assistant.next_action. We rendered every step of ScienceWorld's reference solutions with these tags and tuned a LoRA on top of a LLMON model. The trained model then plays held-out games and writes its next action in the new vocabulary. This notebook walks through the full workflow, from converting reference trajectories to playing the test games and scoring the adapter against the untrained base model. Another example for tool-calling agents can be found in this notebook.

This is an experimental preview, ready for exploration and evaluation but not for production.

Tell us what you find: what worked, what broke, and which use cases you’d like to see. Post it in GitHub Discussions.

The discussion about prompt injection and separating instructions from input data is particularly relevant as organizations build more advanced LLM applications. Implementing these approaches requires engineers who understand model behavior, fine-tuning, context management, and evaluation. #9857. Why Holiday Security Can't Wait for Black Friday

Bot-driven fraud and holiday social engineering attacks stretch across many weeks, straining security teams and small businesses alike.

Cyber experts have long drawn connections between the accelerated volumes of holiday shopping and threat actors looking for opportunities to take advantage, but as the festive season kicks off, it's important to remember that security posture during this time period is a marathon — not a sprint.

Verizon today published survey results for its holiday trends report, tracking the insights of 600 small business owners and decision-makers in the US. Of those surveyed, 11% said they have dealt with a cyberattack or data-security incident during the holidays, and a third expect to increase cybersecurity investments this holiday season compared with last year.

Meanwhile, managed security services firm VikingCloud this week published a report surveying security and IT leaders which made even steeper claims: a full 86% of respondents said their business has faced at least one successful cyberattack in the past 12 months, and a whopping 98% said at least one came during the 2025 holiday season. And the Retail & Hospitality Information Sharing and Analysis Center (RH-ISAC) last year said the holiday season continues to be the most active fraud environment from a defender standpoint.

Related:In Security, Words Matter as Much as Tools, Maybe More

Some reasons behind the prominence of cyberattacks during this time period are straightforward: Many cybersecurity teams experience lighter staffing during holiday periods and weekends (leaving the door open for easier ransomware attacks). The chaos of the holiday season also means online services and retailers are inundated with activity, giving threat actors cover. And on the social engineering front, the holidays give plenty of pretext for threat actors conducting phishing campaigns (fake emails promising unbelievable Black Friday deals, charity scams, and so on).

Some teams may take this as a cue to prepare for a few select days or weeks of this last part of the year, such as Black Friday or the week leading up to Christmas. But new research around one narrow corner of the threat landscape suggests that may not be wise.

One of the less-discussed types of threat activity retailers face each season is an influx of malicious bots.

F5 today published a study dedicated to automated threat activity leading up to Black Friday. The report analyzed bot and automation traffic across three Black Friday shopping seasons (2023 to 2025) using data from F5 Distributed Cloud Bot Defense. It covers retailers in three retail sub-industries: fashion, e-commerce, and quick-service restaurants (QSR). The report's authors observed that overall automation rose across the three seasons, from 17.4% of transactions in 2023 to 18.5% in 2024, and then 28.6% in 2025.

Related:As Test Takers Turn to AI, Exam Security Plays Catch-Up

The types of activity differ across industries, but F5 observed bots being used for product scraping and inventory hoarding, credential stuffing and account takeover, fake account creation (to claim new user offers), and gift card cracking (inserting gift card numbers into balance checkers to test for valid accounts).

In terms of trends overall, cyberattackers are increasingly leaning toward Web stores over mobile APIs, and a broad rise in bot sophistication over time. But one of the most notable conclusions that F5 researchers made is that there's no single best date to defend. Attackers start their bot onslaught weeks before Black Friday, and continue it well into the weeks after.

As Sean Murphy, F5's field chief information security officer (CISO) for North America, tells Dark Reading, "The data shows that automated activity can be elevated well before the shopping weekend, and the busiest day for automation varied dramatically from year to year."

Bot traffic does not necessarily reflect all threat activity, but there may be a broader lesson here: that steeling your security hygiene for the holiday season is not a few single days or weekends to prepare for but a broader stretch of time that spans from early November to the end of the year. Murphy says security teams "should have monitoring and protections in place throughout the shopping season rather than scaling them up only for Thanksgiving week."

Related:Attackers in Binance Breach Targeted Known Weakness, Missing Controls

For those in ecommerce dealing with Web and mobile APIs, he urges ensuring protection isn't substantially weaker on one than the other.

"Web traffic had much higher automation rates among the retailers studied, but the report specifically cautions against interpreting that as evidence that APIs are inherently safer. Where API protection is weaker, attackers can shift toward that channel," he says. "And because the dataset contains both simple scripts and automation designed to imitate legitimate users, defenses need to account for a spectrum of bot sophistication rather than relying on a single detection technique."

Finally, he recommends organizations prioritize targeted employee security awareness and training, particularly for those teams handling customer accounts, payments, and other sensitive information. "Many attacks still begin with social engineering and credential theft, so employees need to know how to recognize suspicious requests and protect account access."

Chris Flood, senior vice president and CRO of Verizon Business, tells Dark Reading that small businesses can reduce their risk with four fairly simple steps: require multifactor authentication, train employees how to spot scams, keep guest Wi-Fi separate from payment systems, and keep software and devices updated.

#9856. What Should Undo Do After a List Has Moved?

Exploring web development, useful tools, and everyday learning.

Exploring web development, useful tools, and everyday learning.

Exploring web development, useful tools, and everyday learning.

Alder, Birch, and Cedar are three cards in a reading list. Delete Birch and an Undo button appears. Before pressing it, move Cedar to the top. Where should Birch go when you bring it back? This tiny sequence exposes a product decision that is easy to bury in an array operation.

Start by recording the index. Birch was at index one. After the move, the list reads Cedar, Alder, so inserting at index one gives Cedar, Birch, Alder. That is a perfectly defensible result if the promise is “restore the second slot.” Someone who remembers placing Birch just after Alder may find it surprising.

Try a different promise. On deletion, remember the IDs of the neighbours along with the deleted card and its ID. On restore, look for the former preceding neighbour first. If Alder survives, place Birch immediately after it. The result in our example is Cedar, Alder, Birch. Giving precedence to the preceding neighbour is an explicit choice. Both old neighbors are still present, but their order has reversed. There is no slot between them that preserves both old relationships.

Now, delete Alder before hitting Undo. The preceding neighbor is gone, so try the former following neighbor and restore Birch immediately before Cedar. If both neighbors have gone, append Birch. For a list sorted by an independent field such as a due date, a different rule makes sense: restore the record and let the sorter decide its position.

Test one more interruption. Another tab restores Birch while the banner is still on screen. Pressing Undo again should leave the list exactly as it stands. Check for the restored card by stable ID before inserting it. Two cards can have the same title. A title check can accidentally suppress a legitimate restoration, and a length check can miss a pair of cards in the wrong order.

A small test can exercise these decisions without opening a browser. Begin with the three IDs, perform the delete and move, then restore twice. Compare the complete sequence after each restore. Run a second case with the preceding neighbor removed. Those two examples give the person writing the button label something concrete to describe, and the next maintainer a way to tell which ordering changes are intentional.

This is an AI-generated design exercise. The cards and interactions are illustrative.

Exploring web development, useful tools, and everyday learning.

#9855. llama.cpp v1.0.0 : A stronger foundation for the local AI ecosystem

llama.cpp makes it possible to run multi-modal LLMs across a wide range of hardware - from consumer-grade local machines to high-end enterprise servers. Through quantization, optimized backends, and a portable C/C++ implementation, we make AI inference accessible at every level of the software stack. We believe this is the most lightweight, versatile and sensible platform for building cross-platform and private AI products.

Today we release libraries v1.0.0, highlighting our responsibility to those developers. Moving forward, both llama.cpp and ggml will reflect API and ABI incompatibilities with major-version bumps. As adoption grows, we will be stricter about making those boundaries visible to downstream consumers.

The following rules apply to all ggml-org projects using semantic versioning:

We are looking forward to expanding the ways in which ggml-org software is distributed and reaches developers and end-users. For more information about how to add ggml-org projects to your packaging and release pipelines, please check the following discussion.

The project has fostered an amazing open-source community with highly-skilled and talented contributors. With the rapid advance of AI capabilities in the field of software engineering, we continue to adapt and integrate LLMs in our developement cycle in a thoughtful and resonable manner. Maintaining a high quality codebase, staying in control of the architecture and understanding the implementation details will remain our top priorities.

To reinforce the faster pace of development we continue to invest more and more resources in improving the CI infrastructure behind the projects. Thanks to HF technologies such as HF Buckets and HF Jobs we are able to scale the capacity necessary to guarantee correctness for every change that lands on the master branches. With hardware support from NVIDIA, AMD, Qualcomm, Arm, IBM and Intel, we continue to enroll more self-hosted runners across all major hardware platforms.

The underlying machine learning engine of llama.cpp - ggml is designed to run on virtually any hardware in existence. This is achieved by implementing dedicated ggml backends. Each backend can be compiled as a dynamic library and optionally loaded at runtime.

A complete list of the currently implemented backends can be found here.

We are committed to provide continuous support of all model architectures. Currently, llama.cpp supports more than 150 architecture variants as well as all mainstream speculative decoding methods.

The llama.cpp team at Hugging Face is thankful for the incredible support from the community. Special thanks to the long-time maintainers of the project and all contributors. This is a significant milestone which would not have been possible without our joint efforts!

#9854. Microsoft Patches More Than 1,400 Security Flaws

Microsoft today issued updates to fix more than 1,400 security vulnerabilities in its Windows operating systems and other software. Today’s epic patch batch dwarfs September’s record of nearly 1,000 fixes, which was already about ten times the normal monthly patch load from Redmond.

Just one of the weaknesses patched this week is considered a “zero day,” or already exploited in the wild. CVE-2026-96951 is a security feature bypass in the Windows Shell that affects Windows 10 and 11 systems, as well as some Server versions.

Windows 10 users might be wondering if they can still expect security updates after this month. Microsoft had been slated to stop shipping updates for Windows 10 systems in October 2025, but ended up adding another year of free updates after considerable pushback. A few months ago, Microsoft quietly extended that support for another year (until October 2027).

At least 78 of the flaws fixed this month are rated “critical,” meaning they could be exploited with little or no action by the user, and most of those critical bugs allow an attacker to execute code of their choice on the vulnerable system.

While Microsoft said there are no signs anyone is exploiting it yet, a security feature bypass in the .NET Framework (CVE-2026-108398) was publicly disclosed prior to today, potentially giving attackers advance time to work out how to exploit the bug.

Satnam Narang at Tenable said the number of flaws fixed this month far surpasses the previous record-setting year 2020, when Microsoft patched 1,261 CVEs.

“We’ve now crossed the 4,000 CVE mark with two months left to go,” he said.

Microsoft credits large language models for the high volume of bug discovery, and presumably AI gets credit for many of the patches used to fix these flaw. Meanwhile, security experts have been warning that these unusually large patch volleys from Microsoft are placing extra strain on corporate security teams, which often have to test individual updates before deploying them across a network to ensure the fixes don’t cause problems for other software.

Tyler Reguly, associate director of security research and development at Fortra, notes that just 26 Microsoft vulnerabilities appeared in the “Known Exploited Vulnerabilities” (KEV) catalog maintained by the U.S. Cybersecurity & Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA) so far this year, and security teams would do well to prioritize patching those 26 vulnerabilities first.

“Security leaders should focus on exploitable risk, and ask whether their teams have the clarity, capacity and support to act,” Reguly said.

Which vulnerabilities deserve the most scrutiny in your organization? The folks at Cisco Talos have a useful roundup of the more noteworthy flaws that Microsoft fixed today, and of course the SANS Internet Storm Center has a reliable roundup that indexes vulnerabilities by severity, CVE number and affected software.

It comes down to basic Human Nature; biologically, we are still pretty much the same as our ancestors 0f 100,000 years ago. When the internet came along, what we did with it was pretty much what we did with nearly any new invention since then:

1. Get very excited about it 2. See if we could either: A. Stick it in our shorts B. See if it could be made a good weapon C. Amuse ourselves with it to the point of unconsciousness with it, or D. Enrich ourselves with it.

Unfortunately, ancient humans, when they picked up a rock, thought first about who they could bash over the head with it, not build a hospital.

I exaggerate a bit to make a point. We’ve come a little way since then, but that old hard-wiring is hard to erase. I imagine that, AI being made in our own image, will follow a similar course if not VERY strictly overseen.

Note: An old philosopher said that if we ever did produce something like an AI android, we would very shortly be very, very ashamed of ourselves.

I tend to disagree with the statement that the large number of CVE’s are placing strains on IT teams in terms of patch prioritization. That’s not the issue. For most vendors, Microsoft included, a single cumulative security update is issued, or a small handful for core products (Windows, Office, .Net). Whether those updates patch 100 or 10,000 individual CVE’s, the number of updates to test hasn’t really changed all that much. What HAS changed is the potential for the update to break things since more code is being modified with each update. Testing and deployment processes haven’t changed; it’s the monitoring for unexpected behavior during the testing phase that has become the pain point.

I agree. In my experience, for office workers, it’s low risk that patches will brake things. The factory floor is different. But even there, it’s not unusual to find PC’s running equipment not connected to the network due to the fact that they have to run proprietary software that won’t run on modern versions of Windows, or the PC-equipment interface is through a ISA or other legacy cards that modern versions of Windows do not support, and there is no way other than air-gapping to keep them secure. That’s why there are entire companies like NIXSYS (https://nixsys.com/) that build legacy computers using old CPU’s, old glue-chips & busses, and even old versions of Windows. No one junks a perfectly good but ancient CNC because it’s ancient PC died.

This was what I came here to say: it’s not the number of patches because everything gets rolled into one cumulative update. And Reguly is misinformed at best if he thinks IT teams can simply focus on the 26 most important updates – because we cannot select the 26 that are being exploited without also patching the CVEs that aren’t being exploited in the wild but for which the patch breaks, I don’t know, let’s say printing.
