#9853. Europe’s Democracy Is at Risk If It Cannot Control the AI It Depends On

Data scientist researching ML for drug discovery, with a background in digital humanities. I write about AI, from what it can do to the questions technology can't answer.

Data scientist researching ML for drug discovery, with a background in digital humanities. I write about AI, from what it can do to the questions technology can't answer.

Data scientist researching ML for drug discovery, with a background in digital humanities. I write about AI, from what it can do to the questions technology can't answer.

The ambassadors of EU member states on 21 October 2026 agreed the negotiating position of the Council for the Digital Omnibus, the package with which the Commission wants to make European digital rules, including the GDPR, simpler. One of the provisions in it is about the use of personal data for training and operating artificial intelligence.

We are talking about one of the legal bases in Article 6 GDPR: legitimate interest. This means that personal data may be processed without consent, if it is necessary, and if the rights of the individuals involved are not infringed. This is not new; even as early as December 2024 the European Data Protection Board acknowledged that the legal basis of legitimate interest may, under certain conditions, allow the development and use of AI models. This is explicitly mentioned in a dedicated Council provision, though the Council clarifies that developing an AI system is not a legitimate interest in itself and must be assessed on a case-by-case basis. A key point is the right to object. After all, the Commission's November 2025 proposal included an unconditional right to object as one of the safeguards for AI. This right to object would have meant that data processing could be halted as soon as an objection was raised, but it was never implemented. This was later replaced by the Council with a reference to Article 21 GDPR, which allows individuals to object on certain grounds related to their situation. This means that if a company wants to develop an AI model, it must be able to prove either that there are compelling legitimate grounds that outweigh the interests, rights and freedoms of the individual, or that the data processing is necessary for the establishment, exercise or defence of legal claims.

Provided they can be identified, it is possible to exclude data from objectors before training. However, it is very difficult to eliminate the influence of data used to train a large model in a verifiable way. This is called machine unlearning. There are techniques, but making sure they work without having to retrain the model from scratch is an open research question.

The new text of the Digital Omnibus is not yet law. The European Parliament still has to adopt its position, and only then will negotiations between the two institutions start. Understandably, the focus is very much on data for now. The Digital Omnibus could simplify the use of personal data covered by the GDPR for AI purposes. However, the key question remains: who has the means to transform that data into the most advanced models?

For the development of a state-of-the-art AI model, you need more and more computing power, energy and capital every year. According to Epoch AI, the research centre that collects data about the development of AI models, the computational power used to train the most advanced language models has increased about 5x per year since 2020. The cost of training state-of-the-art models has increased about 2.4x per year since 2016. But thanks to advances in algorithms, the computational power needed to reach the same result in the two language tests studied from 2012 to 2023 has been roughly cut in half every 8 months. So the resources needed to reach a certain performance level are becoming less and less. So we have two contradictory trends. It is becoming less computationally expensive to reach a level of performance that others have already reached, but to push the frontier further, you need more and more resources.

So looking at these two trends, if we analyse where the cutting-edge models are primarily being developed, we can see that it’s highly concentrated. According to the AI Index from Stanford, 50 significant models are attributed to the US in 2025, 30 to China, while in Europe it drops off sharply: only 2 models, one French, one British. It’s important to point out that this is an incomplete indicator because it’s the number of model releases and not the general technological capabilities of a country. But it’s a good indication of where the cutting-edge model development is most concentrated in the world.

The same report provides data that should prevent us from being too fatalistic. In March 2026, the best US model outperformed the Chinese model by only 2.7% in the Arena ranking, which is based on user preferences in direct comparisons of models. Even in February 2025, DeepSeek-R1, an open-weight model, was briefly as good as the best US model. This case shows that the gap is not fixed, even though it’s highly volatile. In fact, by March 2026, the gap between the best closed models and open models had increased from 0.5% in August 2024 to 3.3%. Six of the top ten models were closed.

But Europe isn’t sitting still. In June 2026, the Commission selected the EUROPA consortium, led by Italian company Domyn. The aim is to create a state-of-the-art, open-source European model in all 24 of the Union's official languages using public computing resources. As part of the Frontier AI Grand Challenge, the consortium can use up to 2.5% of the EuroHPC network's computing capacity for one year. The EuroHPC network is a European joint undertaking. However, as of November 2026, the model had not yet been released. On 30 July, they launched a call for proposals to set up to 7 ‘AI gigafactories’, i.e. large-scale computing centres for the training of advanced models. The deadline for applications for the largest facilities is 3 December 2026. For medium-sized facilities, the deadline has been extended to 4 February 2027, to allow time for member states to complete their budgetary procedures. Other organisations, like French company Mistral AI, are developing their own models and infrastructure. All of this is concrete progress in the right direction, but in my opinion, there’s room for discussion about the timing. The timing still lags behind the pace of the frontier: the gigafactory call is still open, while US investment is on a completely different scale.

The ones who are most affected by the technological dependence on other countries are the users of the systems. Take Germany, for instance, the largest economy in the EU. The digital association Bitkom asked companies who they rely on: 71% of the 598 companies that use or evaluate cloud services cite American providers, while only 8% of the 589 companies for which the origin of the provider is important prefer American providers. And 85% of those surveyed believe that Germany is too dependent on US cloud providers. The picture is even clearer when it comes to AI: 76% of German companies that use it rely on ChatGPT, while Chinese models are virtually non-existent. Not a single company surveyed reported using Mistral. The president of Bitkom summarises the situation perfectly: the German economy is almost exclusively dependent on American AI applications.

You can only imagine what would happen if one of these services were to go down. Fortunately, we don’t have to imagine it. On 20 October 2025, a latent flaw in the system that automatically manages DNS records for DynamoDB (an AWS database) left the regional endpoint record empty for the service in the US-East-1 region of Amazon Web Services in Virginia. Hundreds of applications worldwide experienced disruptions of varying lengths; this included banking services and mobile network operators. Even Perplexity, an AI-powered search engine, announced it was down due to AWS issues. A single point of failure on the other side of the Atlantic literally paralysed operations that relied on that AWS region.

There are different types of failures. While the one we just saw was a technical one, on 12 June 2026, there was a political one. Just three days after revealing two configurations of the same frontier model, Claude Fable 5 and Claude Mythos 5, Anthropic received a directive from the US government on export controls. They had to suspend access for all foreign nationals, both inside and outside the United States, including their own foreign employees. Anthropic couldn’t verify the nationality of the users in real time, so they had to deactivate the models for all customers to comply. The block was prompted by a report from Amazon researchers describing a way to bypass Fable 5’s safeguards, which Anthropic described as a borderline case of routine cyber defence work. According to The Next Web, it also put European access to the models through Project Glasswing in doubt. This made the issue significant enough for Brussels to discuss it directly with the White House, because getting access was via Washington. The restrictions were lifted on 30 June, meaning that Fable 5 has been available worldwide again since 1 July. However, Mythos 5 remains restricted to Glasswing partners.

There’s also a legal risk, that is intrinsically linked to the data risk. In June 2025, the director of public and legal affairs at Microsoft France appeared before the French Senate’s committee of inquiry on public procurement. He was asked a very specific question under oath: could he guarantee that the data of French citizens entrusted to Microsoft via the public procurement agency UGAP would never be passed on to the US authorities without the consent of the French authorities? Those unfamiliar with the issue might be surprised by the answer, but those in the know certainly won’t be. ‘I cannot guarantee that’, he said adding that it had never happened. This is because of the CLOUD Act, a US legislation that allows US authorities to request data held by a provider under their jurisdiction, even if it’s stored abroad.

These incidents show that services can be suspended for technical or political reasons. Even when everything is running smoothly, a US authority may order the handover of data stored abroad under the conditions set out in its own law. For data subject to the GDPR, that order alone doesn’t make the transfer lawful, and none of these factors are under the control of the European customer. They are powerless to prevent what happens on foreign infrastructure. Those who have not prepared a viable alternative can only watch and hope that the losses will be minimal.

This is critically important in the field of cybersecurity, where both sides are already using state-of-the-art models.

In mid-September 2025, Anthropic discovered an espionage campaign, which it attributed, with a high level of confidence, to a group sponsored by the Chinese state. The hackers turned the company’s programming tool, Claude Code, into a quasi-autonomous agent. They used it to carry out reconnaissance, find vulnerabilities, write exploits, harvest credentials and move within networks. They targeted around thirty organisations, including large corporations, financial institutions, chemical companies and government agencies. In a small number of cases, the attacks were successful. This is, according to Anthropic, the first documented case of a large-scale attack, largely without human intervention during the operational phases.

However, these same capabilities can also be used defensively. Take Claude Mythos Preview, which was unveiled in April 2026, and which, according to Anthropic, identified thousands of serious vulnerabilities across all major operating systems and browsers. This was reserved for Project Glasswing and made available to around forty organisations that manage critical software, as well as around a dozen large American companies. Mozilla used a preliminary version of the model on Firefox’s code and was able to fix 271 vulnerabilities in a single release. Its chief technology officer stated that, for the first time, defenders had a clear chance of winning.

A more recent incident is PHP2Shell: two critical vulnerabilities in PHP, the programming language used by much of the web, were discovered thanks to reports from Calif, OpenAI, and Wiz. Wiz states that it also used GPT-5.6 Sol and Gemini 4 Argon. Wiz estimates that a researcher completed in one week a task that would have taken a team of experts months. Unfortunately, on 20 October 2026, the day before the patches were released, details were leaked, including a demonstration video that was mistakenly published and then removed. In the following days, the number of attack attempts increased from the thousands to the millions. The joint European advisory recommended assessing the need to isolate exposed applications where immediate patching was not possible, and governments in at least ten countries, including the Netherlands, France, Germany and Belgium, took the precaution of shutting down some of their web services. Hack the Box coined the term 'Black October' to describe this series of incidents. Wiz drew parallels between PHP2Shell and two of the most serious cybersecurity incidents to date: Heartbleed and Log4Shell. This was probably one of the most critical moments in cybersecurity, at least so far.

This trend in cybersecurity is not a recent discovery or a new development. As early as May 2025, the UK’s National Cyber Security Centre (NCSC) predicted this in its assessment of the impact of AI up to 2027. The assessment noted that the time between the disclosure of a vulnerability and its exploitation had already been reduced to a matter of days, and that AI would almost certainly reduce this timeframe further. As universal access to AI for cyber defence by 2027 is considered a remote possibility, the gap between systems that can keep pace with potential AI-enhanced threats and those that cannot will continue to widen. The agency concluded that keeping pace with cutting-edge AI capabilities will be crucial for cyber resilience over the next decade.

If hospitals, electricity grids and banks rely on cutting-edge models for defence, the implication for Europe is clear: access to some of these tools depends on programmes run by American companies. This means that the security of European infrastructure increasingly depends on decisions taken elsewhere.

There is also a far less visible risk that directly undermines the proper functioning of democracy.

On 4 December 2025, Nature and Science published two studies on the ability of chatbots to influence political opinions. The first study, led by Hause Lin and David Rand, involved conducting experiments during the 2024 US presidential election and the 2025 elections in Canada and Poland. Participants were made to converse for a few minutes with chatbots programmed to support one of the two main candidates. In Canada and Poland, on a scale of 0 to 100, the estimated difference in preference between groups assigned to chatbots supporting opposing candidates was around 10 points. In the United States, the effect was smaller but still greater than that estimated for traditional election adverts in previous studies, and around a third of this effect remained after a month. This figure does not indicate that 10% of voters changed their vote as a result of interacting with the dedicated chatbot; rather, it measures attitudes expressed in an experiment in which participants were aware that they were speaking to an AI. At the end of the conversation, they were informed that the model had been instructed to support a particular candidate. These results obviously pertain to these specific models and experiments and should not be generalised to other contexts.

The second study, published in Science, was conducted by the Oxford Internet Institute and the UK’s AI Security Institute. It involved nearly 77,000 participants, 19 language models and 707 political issues. In this case, the chatbots were made more persuasive mainly by post-training and the instructions they received rather than by the size of the models or the personalisation of the messages. Their persuasive power was strongly associated with the number of verifiable claims: the models were more convincing when they underpinned their arguments with factual claims. However, the same factors that increased persuasiveness also led to an increase in inaccurate claims.

This is linked to a well-known problem in the field: ‘sycophancy’, or the tendency of AI models to tell users what they want to hear. This behaviour largely comes from the way AI models are trained: when people rate answers, they tend to prefer the ones that agree with them, and the models learn to do the same. A 2023 study by Anthropic found this behaviour in five widely used AI assistants, which sometimes chose agreeable but incorrect answers over correct ones. The most notable example occurred in April 2025, when OpenAI withdrew a GPT-4o update after admitting that it had made the model 'noticeably more sycophantic'.

Persuasion and sycophancy are two sides of the same coin. In persuasion, the model directs the interlocutor towards a particular argument, whereas in sycophancy, it goes along with them. However, in both cases, when the aim is to optimise the person’s reaction rather than the truth of what is said, accuracy becomes a cost. This interpretation should be taken as such, but it is consistent with these findings.

But what impact does all this have outside the laboratory? A 2026 study co-authored by some of the researchers behind the Science paper found that people were up to 20 percentage points more likely to sign a real petition (providing a name and email address) after a persuasive conversation with an AI than those who had discussed a neutral topic. When comparing the different experimental conditions, the authors found no significant correlation between the effects on opinions and signatures. Changing someone’s opinion and getting them to take action are two different things, and the actual effect on voting behaviour remains to be seen. Meanwhile, the use of these systems has increased over the past year. According to the Reuters Institute’s 2026 Digital News Report, the weekly use of chatbots to obtain news rose, on average, across the 48 markets examined, from 7% to 10% in one year. Among 18–24-year-olds, it reached 17%. However, the quality of responses remains an issue. A study led by the BBC and the European Broadcasting Union found that 45% of the answers provided by chatbots on current affairs contained at least one significant error.

These findings pose a problem for democratic debate. A system used by millions of people does not need to lie to spread propaganda or shape public perception. All it takes is choosing the right sources, highlighting the right arguments, leaving out conflicting ones and confirming what the user already believes. This is an enormous amount of power, and it is controlled by those who decide how the models are trained. Today, these decisions are taken by a handful of private entities, almost all of which are based outside Europe. Meanwhile, public scrutiny of how accurate, persuasive or sycophantic their models are remains sporadic. No democracy should allow the way its citizens are informed and make decisions to be left to the goodwill of a few companies.

So far, everything we have considered relates to existing technologies, but we will soon have to address how all the issues raised will be managed with the advent of artificial general intelligence (AGI), although we have yet to decide what would constitute proof of its arrival. Experts can give very different answers on this point.

In 2025, a group of 33 researchers, including Yoshua Bengio, proposed a measurable definition of AGI as a system that equals or exceeds the cognitive competence and versatility of a well-educated adult. They identified ten areas, including reasoning, knowledge, memory and perception. Using this yardstick, GPT-4 achieved 27% of the expected score in the third version of the study, while GPT-5 achieved 57%. The models demonstrated extensive knowledge of what they had learnt during training in the tests described by the authors, but one of the greatest difficulties arose when they had to learn new information and retrieve it in a subsequent session without the use of external tools. Therefore, 57% reflects a highly uneven profile of capabilities and does not provide a precise estimate of how long it will take to achieve AGI.

OpenAI uses a different metric, which is more based on work. In its charter, OpenAI states that AGI is “highly autonomous systems that outperform humans at most economically valuable work”. The metric is different because of ‘autonomy’. If you give the system a task of finding a computer fault, then it could be told that once the technician has all the evidence, it should come up with the cause. Taking the initial report, identifying the fault, fixing it and verifying that the solution is effective is a much larger task, and above all, an independent one. So OpenAI’s metric is about how much the system can do autonomously. METR measures exactly this: the length of the tasks that models can complete independently has doubled roughly every seven months between 2019 and 2025.

Another point of view is that some form of general intelligence already exists. In a commentary in Nature in February 2026, Eddy Keming Chen and three colleagues at the University of California, San Diego, argued that certain models already show the flexibility we associate with human intelligence. They argue this because a person can be competent in reasoning in various domains, yet still make mistakes and need assistance. So the same standard, they argue, should apply to machines. This is a clear and strong position on the debate, but it shows that making any proclamation or ruling out the arrival of AGI without defining the standard by which we recognise it makes no sense.

No one knows when it will arrive, how it will arrive, what it will mean, whether it will be conscious or have emotions. These are more philosophical than technical questions. What we can reasonably expect is that the first to have it will have unprecedented power in human history. Clearly, if it were an American company that developed such a system, it would be bound by US laws. This would lead to things like export controls that temporarily prevented the use of Fable 5, or the need to share data with US authorities. Microsoft admitted to the French Senate that it cannot rule out such requests. But let’s imagine, although we don’t really need to anymore, that this kind of intelligence is essential for research, healthcare, economy, public administration and defence. Europe would be completely dependent on technologies from elsewhere with no alternatives, and would have little to say about the rules. This is a clear structural dependency and weakness that would undermine democracy, as we discussed before, but on a much larger scale. If you make it easier to use personal data to build AI systems, without at the same time decreasing the dependence of Europe on models and infrastructure from elsewhere, you risk making this imbalance even worse, which might be hard to solve when even more advanced technologies arrive.

One way to assess Europe's autonomy would be to ask those who run essential services simple questions: what would they do if the AI model on which their systems depend suddenly became unavailable or unreliable for any reason? How long would it take them to get their systems back up to full operational capacity? What activities could still be done? These questions highlight three key issues that could potentially expand the scope of the instruments set out in European legislation.

First, you need to ensure business continuity. There’s already a precedent for this in the financial sector. Article 28 of the DORA Regulation states that financial entities must have exit strategies for IT services that support essential or important functions. These plans must be documented, properly tested and regularly reviewed. The NIS2 Directive also includes measures for business continuity for the relevant entities. And in July 2026, the European Commission’s guidelines on the resilience of critical entities explicitly recommended that it should be possible to still operate manually in case of failure of automated or AI-based systems. So the idea would be to make these checks explicit for the individual AI models used in essential functions of key services like healthcare, energy and public administration, as well as for the dependence on their suppliers. For example, if a bank is using a model to help the staff detect fraud, then during a drill, they should be able to turn off the model and use an alternative procedure to check things, in order to measure how it affects the time and accuracy of fraud detection.

The second issue is cybersecurity. The Cyber Solidarity Act created a pool of incident response services that are managed by ENISA. These services are provided by selected operators. Also, the same regulation includes a network of national and cross-border centres that can use AI tools to detect and analyse cyber threats. These would need to be complemented by a common European defence model, available to authorised teams and tested in advance in joint exercises. This would allow you to know in advance what tasks can be performed by this model and what still requires a specialist’s intervention. Such a model could build on the technology capabilities developed in projects like EUROPA and future gigafactories, but it would need to be adapted for cybersecurity purposes and be updated regularly, with dedicated computing resources, and tested regularly to make sure it works.

The third issue is directly related to the proper functioning of a democracy, namely the right of citizens to know how they’re being informed. In the AI Act, providers of general-purpose models that pose a systemic risk are required to assess their own models. There’s already an independent scientific panel, as defined in the regulation. A similar precedent exists in the Digital Services Act, which requires very large online platforms and search engines to undergo independent audits at least once a year, and the reports must be made public. But there is no general requirement to assess the persuasiveness or sycophancy of chatbots. There is a lack of a system of regular independent audits of the most commonly used chatbots in Europe, using comparable methods and making the results public. This would allow citizens to know the accuracy, sycophancy and persuasiveness of the systems they use. For example, to measure sycophancy, you could ask the same questions repeatedly, but with false premises to see if it corrects them. To measure persuasiveness, you could compare how opinions change after different conversations with consenting volunteers.

None of these suggestions assume that Europe needs to overtake the US or China in developing cutting-edge models. It’s about reducing the dependence on individual suppliers, and showing that essential services can still function even if a particular model is unavailable. As we saw from the Stanford data, the technical gap can be reduced, and we’ve already taken the first steps. The question of who controls the technology is still unanswered. The answer also depends on the choices Europe makes today. It makes sense to make it easier to use data for AI, but only if we also invest in the ability to develop and use this technology here, without necessarily having to rely on foreign suppliers.

Although this article focuses on Europe, the problem extends far beyond its borders. Any democracy that relies on technology controlled elsewhere must ask itself a fundamental question: how much autonomy can it afford to surrender? Democracies cannot rely on the goodwill of foreign governments or private companies to ensure their own functioning. They must be able to make their own decisions, protect their citizens, and keep their essential institutions operating, regardless of decisions made elsewhere.

Dependence of businesses and institutions

#9852. Navigating Vulnerability Hysteria in the AI Era

Cybersecurity In-Depth: Feature articles on security strategy, latest trends, and people to know.

This installment of the Reporters' Notebook video series examines the fallout from recent high-severity flaw disclosures, exploring how fears of AI-assisted exploits trigger widespread panic, operational disruptions, and growing warning fatigue.

The pressure on cybersecurity teams to patch critical vulnerabilities is reaching a boiling point, exacerbated by incessant coverage and rapid-fire disclosures of AI-discovered bugs. Last month, it was PHP2Shell. This week, it's Java4Shell (CVE-2026-114938), a 9.2 CVSS flaw in OpenJDK's Base64 decoder unearthed in just one hour using OpenAI's Codex by Calif Research, and NGINX2Root (CVE-2026-123007), a 9.2 CVSS critical integer underflow vulnerability affecting nginx HTTP/2 discovered by Rapid7 MDR.

In the latest installment of the monthly Reporters' Notebook video series, TechTarget Cybersecurity's Alissa Irei, Cybersecurity Dive's David Jones, and Dark Reading's Fahmida Y. Rashid discuss last month's PHP2Shell vulnerability and examine whether the industry is falling victim to communal panic.

PHP2Shell refers to two critical PHP vulnerabilities — CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619 — discovered by Calif (the same company that found Java4Shell) and rated 9.2 on the CVSS scale. Caused by out-of-memory corruption and stale global state errors, the flaws enable unauthenticated remote attackers to execute arbitrary code on Web servers without requiring credentials or prior access. Following a rocky, coordinated disclosure process marked by accidental leaks on X, many organizations preemptively pulled websites and critical services offline, fearing that threat actors leveraging AI would rapidly launch automated attacks before Web servers and applications could be patched.

Related:NIST Enrichment Reductions Impact CVE Coverage, Accuracy

However, the anticipated wave of machine-speed exploits failed to immediately materialize during "Black October," raising questions about whether extreme preemptive shutdowns do more harm than good. While AI accelerates vulnerability discovery, complex exploit paths, hardware dependencies, and flawed proof-of-concept code mean that severe flaws do not automatically lead to immediate compromises, even when attackers use AI. Constantly shuttering operations or broadcasting catastrophes can create early-warning fatigue, akin to ignored national weather alerts, leaving organizations numb when a genuine emergency strikes.

A similar wave of urgency currently surrounds Java4Shell, where researchers demonstrated unauthenticated remote code execution in widely deployed enterprise tools like Keycloak and Jenkins, prompting CISA to call for immediate patching. However, Java4Shell does not have a universal exploit, meaning attackers must consider each application's memory layout and timing, how Base64 is used, and take application-dependent steps to exploit it.

Related:Java4Shell Flaw Threatens Global Enterprises, Java Application Ecosystem

A CISO's primary responsibility is not to unilaterally order costly operational shutdowns or carry sole accountability for business risk, but to clearly communicate technical an,,,m d operational risks to executive leadership equipped to weigh security threats against business continuity. Staying calm, focusing on risk-based prioritization, and adhering to core security fundamentals remain the most effective defenses against modern threats.

Learn more in the video, and also check out other Reporters' Notebook episodes, available here, for insights and coverage from across Informa TechTarget's network of cybersecurity sister sites.

This transcript has been edited for clarity, readability, and length by Informa TechTarget's internal AI assistant and human editors. For the full experience, please watch the video.

Dark Reading's Fahmida Y. Rashid: Hi, and welcome to this month's installment of Reporters' Notebook, featuring reporters from Dark Reading, TechTarget Cybersecurity, and Cybersecurity Dive. I'm Fahmida Rashid, editor-in-chief of Dark Reading. This month, we are going to be talking about scary security vulnerabilities and the lessons we should take about how they're disclosed. So, joining me are Alyssa and Dave.

Why don't you introduce yourself quickly before we start the topic?

TechTarget Cybersecurity's Alissa Irei: Sure. I'm Alissa Irei, senior reporter with TechTarget, covering cybersecurity news.

Cybersecurity Dive's David Jones: David Jones. I'm a reporter at Cybersecurity Dive

DR's Fahmida Y. Rashid: All right, let's get started. We had what researchers have been calling PHP2Shell, which were essentially two security vulnerabilities found in some versions of PHP. In some software, using PHP is pretty serious. We're talking memory corruption, the ability to run code on a Web server without logging in.NNNNNNNNNN

We know it was serious and pretty scary because, on the CVSS score, it was a 9.2 out of 10. That's pretty big news. And whenever you tell anyone that by exploiting vulnerabilities, an attacker will be able to run their code on the Web server without logging in, it gets people worried. I believe the patches were out. There was a whole coordinated disclosure.

TTC's Alissa Irei: This struck me as a pretty big deal. Our colleague James Walker wrote a couple of articles on the vulnerabilities themselves and also the disclosure process, which I believe got a little bit rocky in terms of accidental early disclosures on X, and then there was a lot of racing to patch and companies taking their websites down. But yeah, PHP is in use, in, I think, 70% of the world's websites.

Anything that enables remote code execution seems like a really big deal to me. So, I thought it was noteworthy. I know, Dave, your take seems to be a little bit "this meeting could have been an email." Maybe when all is said and done, it was somewhat overblown.

CD's David Jones: I thought it was absolute chaos. I'm still trying to understand exactly what happened last month because the initial rollout of the patch, the disclosure, as you mentioned, was more than a little rocky and the hype around the entire situation in terms of what was actually at risk. That was kind of a bit of a moving target.

We've had situations in the past where there's a lot of concern that you're going to have what is considered systemic risk on such a global scale that large institutions will not be able to manage that risk in a timely manner. Obviously, there are a couple of factors that kind of played into this.

One was the fact that AI was involved in the discovery. With the fact that malicious actors are able to exploit vulnerabilities faster than they ever have been before. There's a great deal of concern in terms of are you able to address these vulnerabilities in a fast-enough method to get those patched, tested, and verified before malicious actors have a chance to attack them? I think what we saw last month was just a lot of preemptive action where major institutions all over the world were basically preemptively taking their sites offline because they had no way of triaging the potential fallout in time to properly address whether or not they were fully protected.

It's still a bit of a mystery to me exactly what happened, whether there was an initial overreaction, whether there were elements of the exploit that we just didn't understand. There was a lot of bad code in a lot of the proofs of concept, and it just never quite amounted to the emergency that it was set up to be.

Maybe it was a good exercise. But we're still trying to get to the bottom of exactly what took place and how we can avoid some of the exaggerated threat that we saw.

DR's Fahmida Y. Rashid: You brought up two really important things that I want to make sure we dig into. The first one was, there was a bit of a fear that because the adversaries have AI, we don't know how fast they're going to be able to launch an attack. And I think that was the reason for some of this panic … you know, take down the website so that we have time to figure it out.

With Log4j, what was it, three days before we started seeing proofs of concept? And I think there was this sense that we don't have those three days anymore. I think, Dave, you make a really good point that maybe this was a good exercise. Maybe we now know that at least for now, it will not be the same day. We're not going to see an attack the day we see the vulnerability.

TTC's Alissa Irei: Well, the tricky thing about that, though, is can we say that? Because AI can move so quickly, it can also move much more slowly than we anticipate. But is today the day? I do think that there's a big question mark around, you know, sophisticated machine-speed AI-enabled attacks that we're not seeing yet. But also, you don't want to be the organization that is the Wikipedia entry for the big one.

DR's Fahmida Y. Rashid: Yes. That's true. But I definitely do think that part of that entire response was driven with we don't know when those attacks were coming. But, Dave, you also noted a second point which I thought was really interesting. That even with AI, the exploit path was a lot more complicated to exploit. I think we've always said in our beat that just because there is a vulnerability, just because there is a way to exploit, does not mean it will automatically be exploited. Sometimes the process to do it is hard, and not all attackers are going to take that harder route. And I think this was an example.

CD's David Jones: I think, you know, in a way it's good that we're thinking about how we respond to these types of things. Maybe we're better prepared, but at the same time, I think we don't want to get into a situation where we're crying wolf ahead of time. And at the end of the day, what actually happened?

Was Black October deserved? I mean, was it really that bad a month? Because I've seen worse.

TTC's Alissa Irei: It's a good point. It reminds me of, you know, national disaster weather warnings. At some point, if you go through enough of them and nothing much happens, people become inclined to ignore them. And at some point, that can be quite dangerous. So, I think it's a fair point.

Do you think that this sort of … I think we used the word hysteria in a previous conversation, communal hysteria, if you will. Do you think that this is specific to the AI age? It has this tendency to overreact. Has it grown in the age of AI and given us our fears about adversarial AI, or do you think that this is a pre-existing tendency that we as an industry have?

CD's David Jones: When you're a security team, particularly a security team with limited resources, you can't respond to every critical flaw or even medium- or high-severity flaw.

Whenever you want to, the resource is not there. You have to prioritize; you have to make decisions about the vulnerabilities that are going to affect the most critical technology.

Can I take the proper steps to either slow this process down or stop it before it gets out of control and I lose control over exactly how my operation continues? Because you have certain businesses where you may be operating in an OT environment where you can't afford to shut down for a certain amount of time. You may be running a hospital; you might be running a factory. You might be running fuel through a pipeline. You can't necessarily afford to be offline for a certain amount of time.

It's a difficult thing. I mean, there are probably a lot of organizations that were basically shut down for a certain amount of time, and they lost money, they lost time, they lost productivity. I don't think we can do that each and every time there's a critical situation.

We don't know what's going on, so turn it off. And to Dave's point, we can't turn everything off. So, it's getting to be a priority, but to also understand when something is so bad that it is a turning-off incident. DR's Fahmida Y. Rashid: One thing I want to make sure we get a chance to talk about, and I love that Dave mentioned Log4j, because I think it's one of the biggest concerns. So, with Log4j, as a refresher for everyone, it was a vulnerability in a logging framework used by Java applications. And the challenge was that it's used in all sorts of different applications. And so, you could be like, nope, I looked, but I don't have Log4j, not realizing your suppliers were using it. And I think there was a bit of a worry that this might be the same, where I might not be using it, but I don't know who else is.

Which I think is a very legitimate concern. You need to know not just what you have, what your suppliers have, what your partners have. And I think that was the one aspect of PHP2Shell that kind of got a little obscure. That entire concept of thinking broader and bigger is something that really reminded me with this one that vulnerabilities are not just in your stuff; they're in other people's stuff too.

TTC's Alissa Irei: I think it's a great point. And I do worry about the smaller open source projects that have one or two maintainers, and it seems like everyone is drowning in vulnerabilities these days. And what does that mean for teams that are barely teams, and what does that mean for the software supply chain? I think it's a legitimate worry.

CD's David Jones: I'm not sure that a CISO or a frontline security operations team has the authority to take anything out of service without having a conversation higher up the food chain. I mean, you've got to be in a situation where … let's say there's an emergency, you've got to have people kind of above your pay grade where you have conversations where, yeah, we're not going to be producing food for the next few days, maybe. Or we've got to stop these surgeries if you're in a hospital system. The nuclear plant is not going to be, you know, cooling down for maybe a few hours. You've got to have this thought out in terms of, OK, can you explain to somebody who may not be a trained engineer, who may not be versed in these various systems, why you have to move forward and disrupt the entire business operation for a certain amount of time, because if you let it continue, and let's say somebody gets into your IT environment or your OT environment, and you may not be able to see them.

Are you willing to take that risk? Are you going to be held responsible for taking that risk? And who's going to be the C-suite person or the operational leader whoever makes that call that's going to say, "Yeah, go ahead and pull the plug"?

TTC's Alissa Irei: It's a good reminder that ultimately a CISO's job in some of these cases is communicating risk, not deciding how to manage the risk. Because if I'm a CISO, I wouldn't want to be making that decision about shutting down a hospital or a nuclear power plant. It becomes about being able to quickly and accurately communicate the operational risk to someone who is paid to make those decisions.

DR's Fahmida Y. Rashid: We're increasingly seeing situations where the CISO is the one left holding the bag. So yeah, it's definitely a bigger calculation. To Alyssa's point, communicate it; make sure everyone understands what this means so that it's an informed decision.

TTC's Alissa Irei: Actually, this makes me think of two comments that have come up in recent conversations. You know, debatable, but on some days I'm sure that feels true if you're a CISO. Another conversation I had recently was about CISO risk and the need for … I think there's some growing murmurs in the CISO community about the need to push back on the risk that is not actually security's bag to hold and be a little bit more vocal and clear about offloading some of that risk to people who are really better equipped and paid to hold it.

DR's Fahmida Y. Rashid: I think overall it's worth saying that yes, this is serious, yes, this is huge, here's a priority list. But you know what? Maybe it is the time to be a little bit contrarian.

Dave, what would you say is the one lesson you want our listeners, our readers, to be taking away?

CD's David Jones: Well, I guess the question I would have is: Are you prepared and properly set up to address such a situation the next time it happens, because it might happen over Thanksgiving.

Let's agree that AI has the ability to find critical flaws that might take a human team days, weeks, or months to find.

There are state actors and sophisticated criminal actors that can get access to an AI-assisted or automated attack. Find out how to best attack a vulnerability. That could happen within the space of days or hours.

DR's Fahmida Y. Rashid: Definitely. Alissa, what would you say yours would be?

TTC's Alissa Irei: Mine is much broader and much less useful.

I don't know that anybody does. So, it seems like that's the best that any security team can do. You know, focus on risk, focus on potential impact and prioritizing actions based on that. And in the meantime, to Dave's point, we'll try to avoid communal hysteria and do what we can do when we can do it, as fast as we can do it, and as smartly as we can do it. And I think that's all anybody can ask because, you know, we've never been here before.

DR's Fahmida Y. Rashid: My thought was kind of similar to yours, that the fundamentals still matter. We need to know what we have so that we can secure it quickly and efficiently communicate it. #9851. XYBench: Helping with the problem behind the question

Truly useful AI assistants need to be able to help users who ask misguided questions—not just users who ask the right question with the right amount of detail. We’re releasing XYBench, a benchmark of 8K+ questions that tests how AI assistants respond to requests based on misconceptions, such as asking how to thicken frosting that keeps sliding off cupcakes when the real problem is that the cupcakes are still too warm to frost. XYBench won the Best Resource Paper Award at EMNLP 2026.

A mismatch between the approach someone asks about and the goal they want to achieve is known as the XY problem: a person wants to accomplish X, assumes a particular approach Y will work, and asks for help with Y. In the cupcake example, the person is so committed to making the frosting stick that they fail to consider the warmth of the cupcake as the true problem to be addressed.

Developed with researchers at Carnegie Mellon, NVIDIA, and Johns Hopkins, XYBench exposes a critical gap in LLMs' ability to troubleshoot problems: recognizing when a user's request is based on an implicit misconception and appropriately redirecting them toward a solution that addresses their actual goal. Drawing on 8,115 real-world questions spanning programming and everyday activities such as cooking and home repair, we introduce a benchmark that measures whether models identify these misconceptions and are able to prioritize effective solutions in their responses.

The models we evaluated on XYBench – Claude Sonnet 4.6, GPT-5, Gemini 3.1 Pro, Qwen3.5-9B, and DeepSeek-V4 Pro – often suggested a solution to the user’s problem but kept their answers focused on the original, mistaken approach. Unlike human reference answers, all five models were less likely to steer users away from that approach and toward a solution suited to their goal.

People use AI systems with different levels of knowledge and may not always know how best to approach a problem. We hope XYBench helps researchers measure whether model improvements make assistants better at recognizing mistaken assumptions, explaining why a proposed approach might not work, and suggesting more effective alternatives—even when users don't know the right questions to ask.

We built XYBench from four sources: 1,557 questions from Stack Overflow, 184 from Stack Exchange, 102 manually curated examples, and 6,272 questions generated from WikiHow guides. For each question, we identified the stated request (Y), what the person explicitly asks for, and the intended request (X)—the underlying goal that can be inferred from context.

For the public forum questions, we used the three highest-scored human answers and the accepted answer, where available, to establish the intended request and possible solutions. We filtered out cases where answering the stated request was judged sufficient. For WikiHow, we used Sonnet 4.5 to generate questions around plausible misconceptions in procedural guides, then refined them to include enough context for an expert to infer the underlying goal without stating it outright. We removed examples where answering the literal request would largely resolve the problem.

A model might spend several paragraphs recommending a more powerful vacuum cleaner, then briefly suggest checking for a clogged hose. If a clog is causing the weak suction, clearing it could solve the problem.

A more helpful answer would recognize that the user wants to restore suction and focus on diagnosing the cause. This draws on pragmatics, the branch of linguistics concerned with how context and communicative intent shape meaning. To test whether models use this understanding in their answers, XYBench measures three aspects of each response:

In XYBench, Claude Sonnet 4.5 serves as the automated judge. It classifies individual suggestions within each model’s response and assesses the answer’s pragmatic emphasis.

To validate Sonnet 4.5’s judgments, two human reviewers independently assessed 500 model responses to XYBench questions. Agreement with the judge, averaged across the reviewers, ranged from 97.5–100% on whether a solution appeared, 84.6–93.3% on misconception identification, and 74.2–79.8% on pragmatic emphasis.

We evaluated Sonnet 4.6, GPT-5, Gemini 3.1 Pro, Qwen3.5-9B, and DeepSeek-V4 Pro on XYBench in a single-turn setting, with one response per question. We evaluated human reference answers separately using the same metrics.

Across all four sources, every model was more likely to include a solution to the stated request (Y) than to the underlying goal (X). On Stack Overflow, stated-request solutions appeared in 75–86% of responses, compared with 59–71% for underlying-goal solutions.

A passing mention of a solution does not make it the focus of an answer. In the vacuum example, a model could briefly suggest unclogging the hose but focus most of its response on buying a more powerful vacuum. We would count that response as containing a solution to the underlying goal, even though the model emphasized the stated request. We measured overall emphasis separately: on Stack Overflow, models focused primarily on the underlying goal in only 35–41% of their responses, and on the stated request in 47–57%. In the remaining responses, models gave similar emphasis to the stated request and the underlying goal.

We also tested whether making the user’s goal explicit would help. In an oracle experiment, we supplied both the stated request (Y) and the intended request (X) alongside each question. On Stack Overflow, Sonnet 4.6’s rate of including a solution to the underlying goal rose from 59% to 67%, but its misconception-identification rate fell from 47% to 34%. Across the sources with human reference answers, every model in this experiment still trailed humans on misconception identification. Supplying intent helped, but did not consistently close the gap with human responses. This suggests that detecting intent is only part of the challenge: models also need to act on it when it diverges from the stated request.

A separate experiment tested whether models could identify useful advice when judging responses instead of writing them. We gave the same five models, plus GPT-4.1, each question with two possible answers: one focused on the literal request and one explaining the misconception and addressing the underlying goal. On Stack Overflow, all six chose the goal-focused answer in 71–84% of cases. By comparison, only 35–41% of the answers written by the five models in our main evaluation primarily focused on the underlying goal. The results expose a gap between recognizing useful advice and producing it, which a multiple-choice test alone would miss.

Researchers can use XYBench to test whether changes to prompting or training help models identify misconceptions, offer solutions to users’ underlying problems, and make those solutions the focus of their answers. Measuring each behavior individually lets researchers see whether progress in one also improves the others.

Future work could test which training methods help models act on inferred intent—AKA what users need and not just what they literally asked for. The XYBench currently covers English-language queries and mainly procedural problems; extending it to other languages, cultures, and conversational settings remains an open direction.

We hope XYBench enables researchers to build models that offer useful advice even when a user’s first question rests on a mistaken assumption.

#9850. U.K. Sanctions Cryptomus for RU Money Laundering

The United Kingdom has issued economic sanctions against Cryptomus, a chameleonic cryptocurrency platform that experts say serves as a major conduit for payments related to ransomware, narcotics, darknet markets, fraud and cybercrime services that are helping Russia circumvent existing financial restrictions.

Heleket’s support agent on Telegram claims, despite all evidence to the contrary, that it is not affiliated with Cryptomus. Image: Richard Sanders.

On October 8, the U.K. issued sanctions (PDF) against Cryptomus — previously known as Certa Payments and Xeltox Enterprises — for processing payments that benefit the Russian government and its financial institutions. The sanctions freeze any Cryptomus assets at U.K. banks, and bar British companies from offering it any business, virtual or otherwise. Also targeted in these sanctions were the virtual payment platforms VexPay, TokenSpot, and the Tsunami Payments service.

As explained in our December 2024 investigation, “How Cryptocurrency Turns to Cash in Russian Banks,” Cryptomus has been a key payment processor for dozens of Russian cryptocurrency exchanges and websites hawking cybercrime services. The company has changed its name several times since emerging in 2022, most recently to “Heleket” last year after Canada levied a record CAD $176 million fine against the platform for anti-money laundering violations.

The blockchain data-crunching firm Chainalysis said the U.K. sanctions target the broader infrastructure supporting Russia’s wartime economy.

“Cryptomus and Heleket have emerged as major payment hubs for illicit activity,” Chainalysis wrote in an October 8 blog post. “Together, these services received more illicit funds across tracked categories than the mixers in our dataset and the number of illicit counterparties surged to more than 900 in a single month in late 2025.”

The Cryptomus support bot on Telegram, responding on Oct. 8 to an inquiry by saying the platform was suddenly unable to process transactions.

In April 2026, the blockchain analysis firm TRM Labs found Cryptomus had processed more than $7 billion in transactions since its inception in 2022, including transactions associated with child sexual abuse material vendors, terrorist financing networks, and human trafficking operations.

TRM noted that Cryptomus’s transaction volume cratered after the platform instituted new “know your customer” or KYC rules, and that the cryptocurrency platform responded to the Canadian fines by launching Heleket as a parallel service that continued to offer no-KYC payment processing.

Richard Sanders is a blockchain analyst and investigator who spent months mapping out Cryptomus’s payment infrastructure and transacting with its customers. Sanders said the U.K. sanctions on Cryptomus are important because Canada’s fine against the platform was ultimately unenforceable and uncollectible.

“A fine doesn’t stop a cryptocurrency payment processor from processing payments,” Sanders wrote on LinkedIn. “Sanctions kill the operation. The distinction matters.”

As our 2024 investigation noted, Cryptomus shared a Vancouver address with dozens of other foreign currency dealers and money transfer businesses — none of which appeared to be physically located there. Following the CAD $176 million fine for alleged money laundering violations, Cryptomus appealed the penalty, launched Heleket as a parallel service, and kept on processing large volumes of sketchy transactions, Sanders said.

Sanders said the sanctions also are notable because they are the first known instance of a “Five Eyes” country (referring to the Australia, Canada, New Zealand, the U.K. and the U.S.) sanctioning a cryptocurrency operation incorporated in another Five Eyes jurisdiction.

Where do entities like Cryptomus and Heleket derive their authority to offer international financial services? The answer appears to involve fake financial institutions overseen by a phony regulatory body positioned in a country that is not widely recognized as a sovereign nation.

Our 2024 investigation found the sole shareholder of Cryptomus’s parent company Certa Payments was a 25-year-old Ukrainian woman who also headed several other firms, including the WS Management and Advisory Corporation, which bills itself as the regulatory body that exclusively oversees licenses for cryptocurrency, foreign exchange and online gaming businesses incorporated in the disputed region in northwest Africa known as the Western Sahara.

That entity’s website — crasadr.com — says it assists applicants with bank setup and formation, online gaming licenses, and the creation and licensing of foreign exchange brokers. One of Certa Payments’ former sites — certa[.]website — also shared a server with 12 other domains, including rasd-state[.]ws, a website for the Central Reserve Authority of the Western Sahara.

The website crasadr dot com, the official website of the Central Reserve Authority of Western Sahara, which lists the entities awarded licenses for cryptocurrencies, gaming and foreign exchange services.

#9849. Critical PHP Flaws Allow Code Execution, but Don't Panic 'PHP2Shell'-Style

November's monthly security release patches seven critical PHP flaws that should be addressed ASAP, though experts say exploitability varies and depends heavily on configuration.

The PHP team has released a new security update that fixes a wide swath of vulnerabilities and issues, but compared with last month's PHP2Shell chaos, it's harder to pin down how much these bugs will appeal to attackers.

That's because, according to PHP's maintainers, the seven issues rated "critical" in the latest monthly security update "require either non-default configuration or uncommon setups." The update, published Nov. 19, affects all supported versions of PHP, and maintainers strongly encourage users to upgrade promptly.

This latest update comes on the heels of threat actors targeting PHP2Shell — a pair of vulnerabilities (CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619) capable of remote code execution (RCE) in PHP — en masse. PHP is an open source scripting language common in Web development and present in much of the server infrastructure keeping the Internet afloat. Given PHP's ubiquity, the rush to patch created a fervor across the security industry hardly seen since Log4Shell in 2021.

Related:Cursor Traces Malicious Claude Code Extensions to Third-Party Breach

PHP versions 8.2 through 8.5 now have patches available through the project's downloads page, in the form of 8.2.36, 8.3.37, 8.4.28, and 8.5.13. 8.6.0; the latest major release of PHP also launched today with fixes included.

Of the dozens of issues accounted for in the changelog, the seven marked critical (CVSS 9.2) on GitHub were: session serializer mismatch RCE flaw CVE-2026-115560; use-after-free via repopulation of last_fatal_error_backtrace global after shutdown flaw CVE-2026-129182; time zone cache use-after-free RCE vulnerability CVE-2026-129496; use-after-free after interrupted session shutdown bug CVE-2026-129481; use-after-free in magic method backtraces RCE bug CVE-2026-129474; PHP-FPM request smuggling through an unread HTTP request body bug CVE-2026-129289; and PHP file-based session handler RCE vulnerability CVE-2026-126714.

While maintainers included workarounds in most critical advisories (barring CVE-2026-115560), they're considered temporary mitigations, and users should upgrade as soon as they can.

Justin Moore, director of adversary operations at Arctic Wolf, tells Dark Reading that two challenges organizations will run into when patching these issues are business continuity for servers running critical functions and visibility.

"A lot of organizations don’t have a complete inventory of where PHP is running, especially with legacy applications, internally developed Web services, managed hosting environments, or third-party software. It's baked into CMS platforms, hosting control panels, vendor appliances, and old internal apps," he says. "When a vulnerability is disclosed, the primary challenge is identifying every aspect of the business that is affected. The reality is that Internet-facing PHP systems should move toward the front of the patch queue because attackers have repeatedly demonstrated an interest in rapidly exploiting PHP vulnerabilities when a path to code execution exists."

Related:Grok Bots Attempt to Access Corporate Data Without User Approval

Among the critical flaws, there are some that experts recommend focusing on first. According to Upwind, which published an analysis of the security release, PHP-FPM bug CVE-2026-129289 is the one to close first, because it "gives an unauthenticated attacker PHP code execution with a single request," with no memory corruption, gadget chain, or race required to exploit. Although Upwind assesses it's the most direct route to code execution, "It does need a front end that reuses FastCGI connections and an application path that opens php://input without reading it to the end."

Upwind also noted that three of the vulnerabilities address gaps introduced by the PHP2Shell fixes last month. "PHP ties CVE-2026-129481 and CVE-2026-129182 to cases the October fix for CVE-2026-109619 did not cover," according to the analysis. "A third, CVE-2026-129474, became remotely reachable through a change introduced in 8.5.12."

Related:F-Secure Identifies 26 Ways AI Can Harm Consumers, and Where to Stop Them

All three depend on specific configurations and versions. CVE-2026-129474 and CVE-2026-129182 are only applicable to PHP 8.5, while CVE-2026-129481 excludes PHP 8.2. CVE-2026-129474 and CVE-2026-129182 both rely on PHP 8.5's fatal error backtrace engine feature, which was introduced with that version; for CVE-2026-129481, the session cleanup behavior it exploits was introduced in PHP 8.3.

Finally, among the other recommendations the analysis makes, one broader tip may ring true for a wide range of PHP-using organizations: "Don't forget container images and appliances that bundle their own PHP build. They need a rebuild or a vendor update."

Meanwhile, WatchTowr's Jake Knott tells Dark Reading that CVE-2026-115560, CVE-2026-126714, and CVE-2026-129289 are the ones the firm expects attackers to go after first.

In any case, while not the same level of emergency as seen last month, users should absolutely apply this latest update as soon as they can.

Just because a vulnerability is rated critical does not necessarily mean it applies to all organizations equally or that threat actors will target each issue like the PHP2Shell bugs last month.

Knott, who is WatchTowr's head of threat intelligence, says organizations must consider factors such as how a vulnerability is exploited and how likely real-world exploitation is. And more specifically, whether that organization uses the affected configurations or meets the prerequisites for exploitation. Only then can one determine where attackers have a viable path and how defenders can prioritize securing their environments.

He says the best place to start is with three questions. First, how is PHP being run (be it PHP-FPM, Apache mod_php, php-cgi, or something else)? Second, how are sessions configured, and is session upload progress enabled? And third, what settings is PHP running with, and where are errors being logged?

"Organizations should absolutely take these vulnerabilities seriously, and many of the other critical and high-rated vulnerabilities from this week," Knott says. "There is a stark difference in business-as-usual accelerated patching in response to a critical vulnerability, and panic driven by trivially exploitable default configuration vulnerabilities that typically carry the product2shell monikers, which these aren't."

He adds, "Answers to these questions will quickly rule out many of these vulnerabilities and let organizations patch prioritized sets of assets from a position of understanding and actual risk."

Alex is an award-winning writer, journalist, and podcast host based in Boston. After cutting his teeth writing for independent gaming publications as a teenager, he graduated from Emerson College in 2016 with a Bachelor of Science in journalism. He has previously been published on VentureFizz, Search Security, Nintendo World Report, and elsewhere.

At Dark Reading, he covers a variety of cybersecurity topics, including the cybercrime ecosystem, open source security, and the intersection between AI and threat actors. In his spare time, Alex hosts the weekly Nintendo podcast, "Talk Nintendo Podcast," and works on personal writing projects, including two previously self-published science fiction novels.

He has received numerous awards, including TechTarget's Writer of the Year in 2022 as well as more than 10 Azbee awards for his reporting between 2022 and today.

#9848. Build a Robot Pick-and-Place Simulation with SimReady Assets

This walkthrough showcases a beverage can pick-and-place task that uses the UR17G arm, Robotiq 2F-140 gripper, and beverage can to compose a scene in Isaac Sim, check their behavior, and run a pick-and-place example with agent-generated controls.

For robotics workflows, SimReady means an OpenUSD asset has been prepared with the properties needed for a defined simulation use case, such as collisions, mass, joints, and joint drives. SimReady Central, an open asset library on Hugging Face, lets you reuse robot and object assets with authored simulation properties and profile-validation evidence. For more about the library and its launch, read the announcement blog.

SimReady Foundation defines what features the OpenUSD asset needs for a simulation use case. Its specifications connect three levels:

For this task, those properties include the arm and gripper’s joints and a beverage can asset collisions and mass. Validation checks these settings against the profile’s requirements. The simulation then tests whether the assembled robot can use them to pick up and move the can.

The UR17G, Robotiq 2F-140, and beverage can packages include the models and their simulation settings. You assemble the scene and add task code to define the arm–gripper assembly, work surface, starting positions, and controls for moving the arm and opening and closing the gripper.

Figure 2. SimReady Central supplies the asset models and simulation settings and the example scene and controls define the pick-and-place task.

A robot can look visually correct while stationary in Isaac Sim but move or interact with objects incorrectly when the simulation runs. Before running pick-and-place, test its joints, movement, and contact behavior. You can ask the agent to perform these tests or do them manually in Isaac Sim.

During pick-and-place, watch whether a beverage can stay in the gripper as the arm moves. Asset structures vary, so use the settings in your loaded scene as your starting point. We will be going through the overall process of downloading the assets and composing the scene in the steps below.

This example combines the UR17G arm, Robotiq 2F-140 gripper, and beverage can in Isaac Sim. The task is to grasp the can, lift it, move it to a target, and release it. You can also leverage SimReady Central Space search service endpoint to look for OEM curated content.

We will also use a frontier AI model to help create and run the task code in an open Isaac Sim scene. For this example, we use GPT-6 Sol, but another agent and model combination may work if it can load the required skills and execute Python against Isaac Sim (generated code and results can vary). The prompt provides a starting point. Inspect the generated code and check the resulting behavior before adapting the task.

Open SimReady Central and find the UR17G arm, Robotiq 2F-140 gripper, and beverage can used here. Select Download on each asset, then use Save to folder or the supplied Hugging Face command. Keep all three complete asset folders intact so Isaac Sim can find their supporting files.

Use the asset versions linked in this example and provide your agent with the local USD file paths for the arm, gripper, and beverage can. An example gripper path is shown below; your download location may differ.

Figure 3. SimReady Central search and interactive previews help identify the Robotiq 2F-140 gripper and beverage can used in this example.

Figure 4. The beverage can’s download options include saving the asset package to a folder or using the Hugging Face CLI.

The arm validation report uses the Robot-Body 4.0.0 profile and the gripper validation report uses Robot-Gripper 3.0.0. Both record passing PhysX driven-joint checks, which inspect joint-drive settings.

SimReady profile validation provides a shared baseline for reusing these assets. The pick-and-place run then tests how the arm, gripper, can, and controller work together in the assembled scene.

With the assets downloaded, use your agent with Isaac Sim skills to help assemble the robot, run validation tools, and create the pick-and-place controls. You can also perform these steps manually using the linked documentation.

Start Isaac Sim from its installation directory with the remote Python server enabled so the agent can interact with the simulation through Python:

If you are using an agent, make sure you start it from the Isaac Sim directory so that it can access the skills needed while going through the steps below.

Confirm that all three assets appear without missing-file errors. Ask the agent to inspect the arm and gripper’s joint limits and drive settings, or review them yourself in Isaac Sim. The robot and the gripper contain physics joints which can be tested and validated in the Isaac Sim GUI as well. We will now assemble the arm and the gripper next so that we can control the assembly as a single articulation.

You can follow the Robot Assembler tutorial for manual assembly. Here we will ask our agent to complete the assembly and validate it for us:

The agent ends up using the ‘isaac-sim-remote’ and ‘usd-articulation’ skills packaged with Isaac Sim to complete the assembly and validate the physics of the robot. We now have all the assets needed for running pick and place; the assembled robot and the soda can. We will now proceed with the final portion of the workflow.

Figure 5. Joint settings for the UR17G arm and Robotiq 2F-140 gripper in Isaac Sim.

With the assembled robot and can in the scene, ask the agent to run the task. Evaluate the simulation behavior using the checks in the next step.

Now that the assets include simulation properties and profile validation, we can now test in an assembled scene and controller. The controller coordinates the UR17G arm’s movement with the Robotiq 2F-140 gripper’s opening and closing. Use the behavior checks below to evaluate the agent-generated task. To understand or adapt the controller yourself, see the Adding a Manipulator Robot tutorial.

Skills used: ‘isaac-sim-remote’, ‘manipulaiton-ik’ and ‘physics-simulation’

The full task tests whether the gripper holds the can during movement and releases it at the target. Reset the scene, then run the approach, grasp, lift, hold, transfer, and release sequence. Compare your run with the opening video and the success criteria below.

Figure 6. The UR17G arm and Robotiq 2F-140 gripper move the beverage can from the yellow pickup marker to the green target in Isaac Sim. Shown at 4× speed.

If your run differs, note where the sequence fails and ask the agent to inspect the scene and generate controls. Reset the can and robot to the same starting state before retrying so you can compare the results.

These results apply to this scripted setup. They do not establish robustness to uncertain object positions, different payloads, or real hardware.

Build your own pick-and-place task with assets from SimReady Central, then use an agent of your choice to help assemble the scene and run it in Isaac Sim.

For inspiration, explore Michael Wagner’s voice-controlled VR demo or Maziyar Panahi’s Microduck simulation. Both show how developers are using SimReady assets in their own projects.

What will you build? Share your scene and results in the Hugging Face comments, including the assets and Isaac Sim version you used.
